title: The Data Science Interview in 2026: What’s Changed and How to Prepare
abstract: The Data Science Interview in 2026: What’s Changed and How to Prepare A round-by-round breakdown of how the hiring process has shifted, from AI-assisted coding rounds to GenAI evaluation questions, and what you need to do differently to be ready. By Vinod Chugani on November 4, 2026 in Career Advice The data science interview has changed more in the past two years than in the previous five. If you prepped for interviews in 2023 or 2024 and you're back on the market now, the format you practiced for might not match what you'll actually face. Some shifts are structural. Take-home assignments look different. AI tools are explicitly part of many live coding rounds. Machine learning system design questions, once reserved for senior loops, now show up at the mid-level. Other shifts are topical: generative AI (GenAI) and large language model (LLM) evaluation questions have become their own interview category, and behavioral rounds dig into how you handle AI-generated output, not just ambiguous data. And some shifts reflect a tighter market. Processes run longer, more rounds are common, and the bar for "good" in system design or business case rounds has gone up. That said, a lot hasn't changed. SQL fluency still matters, and in some ways it's tested more rigorously, not less. Statistical reasoning and A/B testing are still core requirements. And the ability to explain analytical findings to a non-technical audience? That's still one of the most commonly cited differences between candidates who get offers and those who don't. This guide covers both sides: what's genuinely changed, and what you still need to prepare. The Modern Data Science Interview Loop A typical data science interview at a mid-size to large tech company in 2026 runs four to six rounds over two to four weeks. The exact combination varies by company type and role, but most loops include some version of these: Recruiter screen (30–45 minutes) Background, motivation, compensation expectations, and timeline. Nothing here has changed dramatically, but the bar for narrative clarity has gone up. Interviewers flag candidates who can't deliver a crisp 90-second summary of their career progression and what specifically drew them to this role. Vague answers like "I want to work on interesting problems" don't land well. Technical coding round (45–90 minutes) SQL and Python, usually in a live shared environment. This is where the AI tool question is most visible. More on that below. Statistics and machine learning fundamentals round (60–90 minutes) Conceptual depth, model selection judgment, and evaluation metric reasoning. Statistical inference, A/B testing design, and the ability to reason about model failure modes come up consistently. Machine learning system design round (45–75 minutes) End-to-end production machine learning system design. This round has grown in scope and now appears in more mid-level loops than it did two years ago. Business case or product sense round (45–75 minutes) Translating a business problem into a data problem, defining what to measure, and explaining the output to a non-technical stakeholder. Behavioral round (30–60 minutes) STAR-format questions on collaboration, ambiguity, stakeholder conflict, and (more and more) situations where AI or model outputs behaved unexpectedly. For GenAI-specific roles, an additional round has emerged: a dedicated evaluation round that tests how candidates design and implement LLM evaluation frameworks. What Has Changed: The Six Biggest Shifts 1. AI Tools Are Now Part of the Interview, but the Rules Vary This is the most visible structural change in 2026. The blanket "no tools allowed" policy that governed technical interviews for over a decade has splintered into three distinct formats. Candidates who don't know which one they're walking into will struggle. Proctored no-tools rounds. Live algorithm and SQL coding rounds at most large companies still prohibit AI assistance. The logic is simple: if the interviewer wants to evaluate your independent reasoning, AI-generated output gets in the way. These rounds now test something slightly different from before. There's less emphasis on syntax recall and more on reasoning about when to use a window function versus a self-join, and why . AI-allowed assisted rounds. A growing number of companies (roughly 25% of U.S. employers as of mid-2026, and climbing) explicitly permit AI tools in at least one interview round. Here, the evaluation flips entirely. The evaluation flips: interviewers assume you can get working code and watch how you check it, fix it, and explain it. Candidates who accept AI-generated code without checking for edge cases, wrong assumptions, or logic errors fail these rounds just as easily as they'd fail a no-tools round through poor logic. Open-ended take-homes with expected AI use. Take-home assessments have evolved, too. Companies now commonly ask candidates to submit their work and then answer a follow-up question: "How did you use AI in completing this?" Some require a live walkthrough where you explain and modify your submission on the spot. That format is essentially impossible to bluff. If you get a take-home in 2026, assume you'll need to defend every decision in a follow-up conversation. The practical takeaway: before any technical round, send one clear message to your recruiter: "Will I be allowed to use AI tools during the live coding round, and if so, which ones?" This prevents surprises and shows you understand that the format matters. 2. Coding Questions Have Become "AI-Resistant" Alongside AI-allowed rounds, the coding questions themselves have shifted. Since AI tools can generate syntactically correct SQL and Python quickly, pure implementation questions have given way to formats that test judgment over generation. The most common new format is debugging AI-generated code. Instead of opening a blank editor and writing a query, you get code that was written by an AI, and your job is to find what's wrong, explain why, and fix it. StrataScratch , one of the go-to interview prep platforms for data science, has added a dedicated "Debug AI Code" mode to reflect this. The interviewer is watching whether you can catch mistakes, understand why they're mistakes, and explain your reasoning. Whether you can produce the solution from scratch is secondary. A second format asks you to explain code you've been given: "Here's a query. Walk me through what it does and why it was written this way." This tests comprehension and communication depth, not implementation speed. Window functions, common table expressions (CTEs), and query optimization are still just as important as before. The difference is that interviewers now expect you to show understanding of the underlying logic, not just demonstrate that you can type the syntax. 3. Machine Learning System Design Has Moved Downstream Machine learning system design rounds used to show up mainly in senior and staff-level interview loops. In 2026, they appear regularly at the mid-level too, driven by the expectation that data scientists own the full model lifecycle rather than hand things off to a separate engineering team. The round tests your ability to design an end-to-end machine learning system from a vague product goal. A typical prompt: "Design a recommendation system for an e-commerce platform handling 50,000 requests per second." A strong response works through six stages: clarifying the business objective, framing it as a machine learning problem, defining data requirements and pipelines, selecting and justifying a modeling approach, designing the deployment and inference architecture, and describing how you'd monitor and maintain the system over time. What's different in 2026 is the content of these questions. Two new categories have become standard: LLM evaluation system design. "Design an evaluation framework for an LLM-powered customer support assistant" is now the 2026 equivalent of "design a data warehouse.

title: 7 Small Specialist Models That Beat Giant LLMs at One Job
abstract: 7 Small Specialist Models That Beat Giant LLMs at One Job Meet seven open specialist models under 10 billion parameters that rival much bigger systems at one job each, from transcription and OCR to routing and speech. By Shittu Olumide , Technical Content Specialist on November 4, 2026 in Language Models Picture a support pipeline built the lazy way. A giant model transcribes the call, reads the attached invoice, pulls out the names and amounts, decides which team gets the ticket, and reads the reply back to the customer. It works, and every step is billed at frontier prices. Most of those steps are single jobs, and small specialist models are built for exactly that. In this article, you will meet seven open models, each under 10 billion parameters, that go head to head with much bigger systems on one task. For each, you get the job it wins, its size and license, the published proof, and code to run it locally. These task-specific models won't replace a giant large language model (LLM) everywhere, and the last section covers where they don't. How These Seven Were Picked Every model had to meet four rules: open weights, one clear job, published proof against something much bigger, and a footprint small enough for a single machine. "Giant" does not always mean "a chat LLM." Where the proof is against a bigger general model, I say so. Where it is against a closed API or a larger specialist, I say that instead. The Seven at a Glance # Job Model Size License What it beats 1 Transcription Parakeet TDT 0.6B v3 0.6B CC-BY-4.0 Whisper large-v3, on accuracy and speed 2 Optical character recognition (OCR) PaddleOCR-VL-1.6 0.9B Apache 2.0 Gemini 3 Pro and GPT-5.2 on OmniDocBench v1.6 3 Entity extraction GLiNER 50M to ~300M Check per checkpoint ChatGPT on zero-shot named entity recognition (NER) 4 Embeddings EmbeddingGemma 308M Gemma terms Open embedding models under 500M 5 Routing Arch-Router 1.5B Katanemo license GPT-4o and Claude-Sonnet-3.7 on routing 6 Decisions Nemotron-Orchestrator-8B 8B NVIDIA License (research only) GPT-5 on Humanity's Last Exam 7 Speech output Kokoro-82M 82M Apache 2.0 Larger open text-to-speech (TTS) models in blind listening tests Setting Up Use a separate virtual environment for each model. These stacks pin different versions of PyTorch and related libraries, and mixing NeMo , Paddle , and vLLM in one environment is asking for conflicts. # One environment per model, for example for the first one python -m venv parakeet-env source parakeet-env/bin/activate # Windows: parakeet-env\Scripts\activate Two models need a little extra. EmbeddingGemma is gated, so accept its license on the model page and log in once: from huggingface_hub import login login() # paste a Hugging Face access token when prompted Kokoro needs the espeak-ng system package ( sudo apt-get install espeak-ng on Ubuntu or brew install espeak-ng on macOS), as its GitHub page notes. That login() call stores your token so later downloads of gated models work without more prompts. Each model downloads its weights on first run, so expect a wait the first time. Let's take a look at the seven models. They run in pipeline order: speech in, documents in, extraction, search, routing, decisions, speech out. 1. Parakeet TDT 0.6B v3: Transcription Size and license : 600M parameters, CC-BY-4.0, 25 European languages with automatic language detection, per the model card . The proof : The Open ASR Leaderboard paper lists Parakeet v3 at an average word error rate of 6.32 against 7.44 for Whisper large-v3, with a throughput of 3,330 against 146 (RTFx, higher is faster). That is about 23 times faster with fewer errors. One roundup puts Parakeet at a quarter of Whisper large-v3's size. Note that this beats a bigger speech model, not a chat LLM. Run it : pip install -U "nemo_toolkit[asr]" import nemo.collections.asr as nemo_asr # Downloads the model on first run; the card says to allow at least 2 GB of RAM asr_model = nemo_asr.models.ASRModel.from_pretrained( model_name="nvidia/parakeet-tdt-0.6b-v3" ) # Pass a list of audio files; 16 kHz mono audio is what the model expects output = asr_model.transcribe(["meeting.wav"]) print(output[0].text) # Add timestamps=True to also get word-level timing # output = asr_model.transcribe(["meeting.wav"], timestamps=True) from_pretrained pulls the checkpoint from Hugging Face and builds the model. transcribe takes a list, so you can batch several files in one call, and each result has a .text field with the transcript. The commented line shows the timestamp option from the model card. The catch : Whisper still covers 99 languages to Parakeet's 25. An October 2026 leaderboard snapshot shows Parakeet ahead in English (5.66% against 6.5% error) but behind Whisper on five of the six other European languages it tracks. 2. PaddleOCR-VL-1.6: Optical Character Recognition Size and license : 0.9B parameters, released May 28, 2026 according to the model card , and listed as Apache 2.0 in a September 2026 OCR roundup . The proof : In the PaddleOCR-VL-1.6 paper , its overall score on OmniDocBench v1.6 is 96.33, against 92.91 for Gemini 3 Pro and 86.59 for GPT-5.2. A 0.9B model is ahead of both frontier systems on document parsing. Run it : # GPU build for CUDA 12.6, as on the model card (use the CPU build from the Paddle install guide if you have no GPU) python -m pip install paddlepaddle-gpu==3.2.1 -i https://www.paddlepaddle.org.cn/packages/stable/cu126/ python -m pip install -U "paddleocr[doc-parser]>=3.6.0" from paddleocr import PaddleOCRVL # pipeline_version="v1.6" selects this release (it needs paddleocr >= 3.6.0) pipeline = PaddleOCRVL(pipeline_version="v1.6") # Accepts a local path or a URL to a page image output = pipeline.predict("invoice.png") for res in output: res.print() # show the parsed result res.save_to_json(save_path="output") # structured output res.save_to_markdown(save_path="output") # readable Markdown, tables included The pipeline runs layout detection first, then the 0.9B model reads each region. One call gives you the page as JSON and as Markdown, which is easier to feed to the next step than raw text. The catch : It is not alone at the top. The same September roundup ranks TeleOCR (96.91) and OvisOCR2 (96.47) just above it on OmniDocBench v1.6, so read "top three," not "number one." The original model card also recommends Windows Subsystem for Linux or Docker on Windows. 3. GLiNER: Entity Extraction Size and license : The NAACL 2024 paper covers models from 50M parameters up. The repo is Apache-2.0, but individual checkpoints differ, and some older ones are listed as CC BY-NC 4.0, so check the checkpoint you pick. The proof : The paper's out-of-domain table has GLiNER-S, at 50M parameters, averaging 52.7 against 47.5 for ChatGPT on zero-shot NER. Its abstract says GLiNER outperforms both ChatGPT and fine-tuned LLMs in zero-shot evaluations. Run it : pip install gliner from gliner import GLiNER # A 90M-class checkpoint; the repo lists this one as Apache 2.0 model = GLiNER.from_pretrained("urchade/gliner_medium-v2.1") text = ( "Sarah Okafor from Brightwave Ltd confirmed invoice INV-20418 " "for $12,400, due on 14 November 2026." ) # You choose the labels at run time; the README suggests title case for v2.1 labels = ["Person", "Company", "Invoice number", "Amount", "Date"] entities = model.predict_entities(text, labels, threshold=0.5) for e in entities: print(f"{e['text']} => {e['label']} ({e['score']:.2f})") The key idea is that labels are just strings you pass in, so you can change what you extract without retraining. threshold controls strictness: raise it for fewer, surer matches. It runs on a plain CPU, as the README says. The catch : The "ChatGPT" in that comparison is the 2023-era model. GLiNER extracts spans of text. It won't reason about them or fill in anything missing. 4. EmbeddingGemma: Embeddings Size and license : 308M parameters, about 100M of them in the model and 200M in embeddings, per Google's announcement .

title: Investigating vault particles with Claude
abstract: Chapter 01 : A vault-like structure in prokaryotes We’re sharing another finding from Anthropic’s biology research lab : the first 3D structure of a vault particle found in prokaryotic cells. Vaults are large, hollow barrels of protein found in cells across the tree of life, and their function is still unknown. Below, we describe how Claude helped at each step of this research: searching across sequence literature, optimizing a method of isolating particles, and mapping the vault’s structure. More information is in our preprint , which we’ve submitted to bioRxiv; we’ll update the link as soon as it goes live. Biological cells were first detected in 1665, but more than three and a half centuries later, much of how they work remains unknown. Until relatively recently, the existence of some crucial components , let alone their function , was controversial. Even today, more than a third of the roughly 4,400 genes in one of the most comprehensively studied cells, the bacterium E. coli , remain poorly understood . Another such enigma is the vault particle . A vault particle is a large, hollow protein shell found in nearly all the cells in our body. It was discovered in 1986 by Leonard Rome and Nancy Kedersha, but its function remains elusive. At roughly three times the mass of a ribosome, it’s one of the largest known molecular complexes in eukaryotes—organisms with complex cells, such as mammals (as opposed to simple, usually single-celled “prokaryotes,” such as bacteria). Vaults take their name from their shape. When observed under an electron microscope, the ribbed shell reminded Dr. Rome and Dr. Kedersha of the vaulted ceiling of a cathedral. In mammals, the shell is made of 78 copies of the major vault protein, arranged as two identical halves joined at the middle. Vaults are found across most of the eukaryotic tree , from slime molds to humans, so scientists believe that they must do something useful. Researchers have proposed various functions, including transporting molecules between the nucleus and cytoplasm , protecting cells from toxic compounds such as cancer drugs , and supporting innate immunity , but none of these proposals have been conclusively confirmed. Other studies have shown that mice lacking vaults still survive , which suggests that vaults may be necessary only under specific environmental conditions. Still, the question remains: why would evolution retain something so large if it didn’t have an important function? Interested in whether Claude could help make progress on this long-standing open problem, our biology research team has been investigating vaults. We haven’t yet determined their biological function, but we did find that many more vault proteins across the tree of life, including those in prokaryotes and the bacteriophages that infect them, can assemble into complete vault-like particles. Related proteins had already been found in the genomes of both prokaryotes and phages, but to our knowledge no one had shown that they assemble into vaults. A vault in a prokaryotic cell gives researchers a simpler system to study. Compared with mammalian cells, bacteria are quick to grow, which makes it easier to investigate where vaults came from, what their basic structure looks like, and what, if anything, they contain. Studying the bacterial relatives of human proteins has been informative before. Bacterial versions of cGAS–STING signaling , gasdermins , and viperins revealed the microbial origins of these human immune defenses. In those cases, their function in humans was already known. For vaults it is not, and their prokaryotic relatives may help reveal it. Here, we describe how we uncovered the molecular structure of a vault from a bacteriophage . Bacteriophages are viruses that infect bacteria. Like all viruses, they hijack their host cells to make their proteins, so this vault would be built inside a bacterium, a prokaryotic cell. The vault is built from 96 copies of a single protein, compared with 78 in human vaults. By duplicating part of the protein, we engineered the vault to be even larger. Together, these results shed light on how such complexes assemble and suggest how they could be adapted for biotechnology —for example, as nanocapsules for delivering enzymes . The cap of the L05 vault. Left: the whole vault, imaged by cryo-EM. Right: its cap seen from above. All 48 chains wind in from the rim toward the tip, overlapping as they go. Two-thirds continue past the first tier and one-third reach the tip, so the cap narrows like a stepped dome. This work also demonstrates our team’s wider aim: to speed up research in fundamental biology by building Claude into every step of the process. Under our direction, Claude searched protein databases, designed the DNA constructs, optimized the isolation method, and processed the microscopy data. As a result, a vault purification that conventionally takes three days took us about 90 minutes, and a first structural model was ready 34 hours later, which we estimate would normally have taken us weeks. Despite this progress, there is still much to be learned about these perplexing structures. When we shared the structure with Dr. Rome, whom we brought on to advise us on this research, he said: Figuring out the function of vaults is still enormously challenging. I am pleased that Anthropic has so much good data. Now, other people will be working on this problem … The broadness of Anthropic’s finding[s] suggests that it is going to be a complicated function and an interesting ride. Our lab is releasing these findings early to continue to show the scientific community how Claude can be used for discovery. You can read more about our results and methods in our preprint , and we will be releasing the structures and additional data soon. A vault-like structure in prokaryotes We uncovered the vault structure using cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM), in which many copies of a particle are flash-frozen and imaged with an electron beam, before being combined into a single 3D model. The vault is built from 96 copies (48 copies per half) of a single phage protein, which we call L05, with a combined mass of about 9.5 megadaltons . By contrast, the mammalian version has 39 copies per half. The phage-derived vault is also shorter and wider: roughly 54 nanometers long and 45 wide, compared with 67 by 40 in mammals. Despite being shorter, it encloses about 25% more volume because it is more spherical. The protein chain that makes up its wall is built from seven repeating segments stacked end to end, rather than the nine in mammalian vaults, and its end caps are flatter. It’s among the largest protein shells ever identified in prokaryotes. One notable feature of its structure is how the caps close. A wall 48 copies around must narrow toward the pole, and it does so in three steps, like a tiered dome. In every group of three neighboring copies, one ends at the first step, one at the second, and one continues to the tip. The three copies are identical along the wall, but take different shapes (conformations) in the cap. Given that we can make this vault in the lab and isolate it quickly, we also experimented with altering its structure to learn more about how these proteins assemble. Working with Claude, we made 15 altered versions of the protein, most with changes at the points where neighboring copies touch. Some single changes near the cap were enough to prevent the shell from closing: in place of sealed vaults we saw open, rosette-like particles, which shows that this region is needed to seal the shell. We also tried making the vault even bigger. Ordinarily, the wall is built from seven repeating segments. When we copied two of them, giving the protein nine—the same number as in the human vault—it assembled into even larger vault particles, increasing the enclosed volume by approximately 20%.

title: New agents and products for security, productivity, and creative work on Claude Marketplace
abstract: We’ve added new agents and products to Claude Marketplace , where teams find partner tools and services to help them get more from Claude. The additions cover security, developer infrastructure, creative, and productivity. Eligible enterprise customers can apply a portion of their committed Anthropic spend toward these solutions. This lets them use one commitment across Claude and partner products, whether they’re buying something new or expanding with a platform they already use. There are now over 25 partner agents and products on the marketplace. Here are the latest additions and what teams can do with them. Products and agents for securing code and systems Chainguard : Chainguard Harness builds applications from source in an isolated microVM and probes the live app for exploitable vulnerabilities. It helps teams fix what Claude finds, with custom remediation recommendations for reproducible vulnerabilities. Checkmarx : Checkmarx One pairs rules-based analysis with AI reasoning to find vulnerabilities in code. It helps teams prioritize findings and fix them before code ships. Cyera : Cyera Agent Guardian inventories Claude deployments, governs permissions before Claude runs, and enforces policy on prompts, files, and tool calls. It helps teams test those controls through red teaming. Rubrik : Rubrik Code Guardian uses frontier AI models from Anthropic to review a secure copy of GitHub or Azure DevOps repositories for multi-step attack paths. It helps security and engineering teams rank issues by severity and turn confirmed critical ones into tracked tickets. Tanium : Tanium Cloud gives teams real-time visibility and control across their endpoints. It helps IT and security teams find and fix vulnerabilities, misconfigurations, and missing patches. Development infrastructure for engineering teams Datadog : Datadog Agent Observability traces agent execution through tools and services. It helps teams improve agent quality, performance, and cost efficiency by surfacing production patterns and recommending fixes. Netlify : Netlify Enterprise deploys apps, sites, and agents to a global edge network, with preview URLs on every change. It helps teams take what they build with Claude from prototype to production with no infrastructure to configure, and includes SSO, role-based access, and audit logs. Tools for marketing and creative work AirOps : AirOps provides an agentic platform for AI search strategy, content, and multichannel execution. It helps marketing teams analyze brand performance in AI search and tie results to pipeline and revenue. Runway : Runway generates and edits video, images, and audio. It helps creative and marketing teams turn a brief into finished assets and edit footage with natural language. Webflow : Webflow provides built-in tools to build, manage, and optimize websites. It helps marketers, designers, developers, and agents make changes, with controls and governance built in. Productivity apps for every team Asana : Asana AI Teammates are prebuilt agents that use context from the Asana Work Graph, each with its own identity, scoped permissions, and audit trail. They help teams handle multi-step work, routing decisions that need judgment to the owner. Glean : Glean connects company knowledge and workflows across systems. It helps employees find answers and complete multi-step tasks across connected apps. monday : monday agents work inside projects, boards, docs, and meetings, using their owners and deadlines as context. They help PMO, IT, marketing, finance, and operations teams control what AI can access, approve, and spend. Zoom: Zoom Agentic Search answers questions inside Claude using the latest meeting summaries, work conversations, documents, and connected third-party sources. Teams get permission-aware results without analyzing raw transcripts or chaining tools together. Get started You can browse all agents and products on Claude Marketplace and request to buy from any listing. If you’re building on Claude and want to join the marketplace, see the ways to join .
