title: How NVIDIA Uses AI Agents to Streamline AI Factory Operations
abstract:
As GPU clusters scale, operations span compute, network, hardware, and scheduling. Site reliability engineers (SREs) often have to examine multiple dashboards to identify the cause of training performance drops. What if a team of AI agents could perform that correlation through one interface? NVIDIA developed the AI Factory Operations Agent to streamline its own internal NVIDIA DGX SuperPOD operations and reduce the manual effort by NVIDIA SREs. Sub-agents communicate through Model Context Protocol (MCP) that any organization can adopt to maximize AI factory uptime and performance. Instead of requiring SREs to check each layer of the AI factory software and hardware separately, the AI Factory Operations Agent uses specialized agents for different operational domains. In production, these agents detect failures, correlate root causes across layers, and surface clear recommendations through a chat interface. SREs can interact with any agent using natural language, switch between investigations, and track every action for auditability. This blog will share learnings and teach you how to implement the AI Factory Operations Agent in your own workflow. The architecture: Using NVIDIA blueprints and open models The AI Factory Operations Agent developer example was built around the NVIDIA NemoClaw blueprint. At the center sits the user-facing agent runtime, which receives SRE queries through a chat interface and invokes the appropriate domain agents and tools. Agents connect to infrastructure through OpenClaw plugins and MCP servers, with each MCP exposing a focused set of approved operational tools. You can work through the built-in web UI or integrate existing coding-agent interfaces through the API. This modular design lets you add new agents and infrastructure integrations without changing the existing agents. The framework is built using NVIDIA OpenShell and is fully on-premises capable, supporting extensibility and data sovereignty. Agent inference uses locally served NVIDIA Nemotron open models, while the framework runs across internal NVIDIA DGX H100, NVIDIA DGX B200, and NVIDIA DGX GB300 production clusters. See the next section for how OpenShell provides agent governance and controls so agents work safely. Figure 1. AI Factory Operations Agent architecture: A NemoClaw agent orchestrating domain-specific agents across GPU cluster infrastructure How NVIDIA built it The AI Factory Operations Agent runs as a Kubernetes control-plane application. Helm deploys the UI, OpenClaw gateway, MCP tool servers, inference endpoint, and NVIDIA OpenShell runtime as Kubernetes services. The chat UI sends each request to NemoClaw, which routes it to the appropriate domain agent. For shell execution, OpenShell creates a per-session Kubernetes sandbox instead of running commands in the main gateway pod. The runtime receives the AI Factory Operations Agent workspace, selected skills, and command policy. Its lifecycle does not modify existing services or production workloads. Security is enforced in layers. Kubernetes inspection uses the server-side run_kubectl tool, which invokes a pinned kubectl binary against registered read-only credentials. OpenShell receives neither kubectl nor Kubernetes credentials. Kubernetes service accounts and role-based access control (RBAC) define the cluster resources the tool can inspect. Because these checks run through the same Kubernetes access path used by the runtime, the results show what the agent can and cannot do inside the cluster. (agent) $ kubectl auth can-i get pods
yes
(agent) $ kubectl auth can-i get configmaps
yes
(agent) $ kubectl auth can-i get secrets
no
(agent) $ kubectl auth can-i create pods
no
(agent) $ kubectl auth can-i update pods
no The AI Factory Operations Agent, sub-agents, and tools Internal NVIDIA deployment of the AI Factory Operations Agent uses a growing ecosystem of NVIDIA data center domain-specific agents, each providing recommendations. Job Recovery Agent: Detects training job failures and goodput degradation; performs multi-layer root cause analysis across scheduler, application, hardware, and network layers; and recommends recovery steps when root cause is confirmed. Hardware Agent: Triages hardware faults at the device level—PCIe errors, ECC errors, GPU issues, NVMe failures, and thermal anomalies—tracing symptoms down to the specific component. Observability Agent: Queries historical Prometheus, telemetry, and integrated Grafana Loki logs to create dashboards dynamically and display them directly in the web UI. Research Agent: Searches preloaded documentation including NVIDIA Mission Control manuals and DGX SuperPOD reference architectures and deployment guides. You can also upload your own runbooks and site-specific guides. Kubernetes Agent: Provides read-only operational awareness across pods, services, deployments, GPU resources, node status, and scheduling state. Cluster Management Agent: Interfaces with NVIDIA Base Command Manager APIs through diagnostic MCP tools for advisory cluster management and troubleshooting. Beyond the domain agents, the framework integrates cross-cutting MCP tools including web search, code execution, and Grafana dashboards. You can also connect your own MCP servers and APIs, adapting the framework to the schedulers, observability platforms, cluster managers, and operational procedures already used in those environments. Learnings from using agents in the data center NVIDIA continues to refine the framework by measuring root cause analysis (RCA) accuracy, tracking SRE agreement, and expanding the agent ecosystem. From production use, five lessons stand out: Clear agent boundaries: Overlapping ownership creates noise, not signal. Read-only first: Accurate investigation builds SRE trust before automation. Cross-layer correlation: The framework connects workload, hardware, and network signals to find root causes missed by isolated tools. Precise MCP tools: Clear tool definitions improve routing and reduce wrong tool selection. Transparent reasoning : SREs need to see tool calls, evidence, and conclusions before taking action. Video 1. AI Factory Operations Agent incident trouble-shooting example, injected into an NVIDIA DGX cluster for internal demonstration. Bringing agent-driven operations to your AI factory For organizations running AI factories at scale, the preferred deployment model is a dedicated GPU-accelerated control plane isolated from the production cluster. The control plane handles agent orchestration and reasoning while the production cluster provides telemetry without consuming training GPUs or disrupting workloads. Internal NVIDIA deployments run model inference on dedicated GPU capacity and use the existing control-plane CPU Kubernetes admin space for runtime services. Other deployments can use a local or cloud inference endpoint based on data sovereignty, cluster size, and available GPU capacity, with smaller deployments using an RTX PRO Workstation or DGX Spark . For multi-tenant AI factories, scoped agents, tools, sandboxes, and Kubernetes permissions control the cluster data, tools, and nodes available to each tenant. Tenant SREs see only their namespaces, jobs, and nodes, while central operations retain broader cluster visibility. Each tenant can use its own set of domain-specific agents and dedicated inference hardware when required. OpenShell enforces these boundaries by running each tenant’s agents and tools in an isolated sandbox with kernel-level restrictions. Get started To get started on streamlining cluster operations management, explore the AI Factory Operations Agent developer example, or access the open source framework and code directly on GitHub . The orchestration framework is available as experimental open source software; APIs, configuration, and deployment requirements may change between releases. NVIDIA customers can contact their account manager to request access to NVIDIA-developed cluster operations agents.

title: NVIDIA CUDA 13.5 Brings NVIDIA Vera Rubin GA Support
abstract:
As artificial intelligence and accelerated computing continue to push the boundaries of what’s possible, the latest NVIDIA CUDA release arrives to unlock unprecedented performance and scale. NVIDIA CUDA 13.5 delivers general availability (GA) across major new platforms. NVIDIA Vera Rubin support moves from early developer access to general availability (GA), ready for enterprise production. Windows on Arm support, GA since CUDA 13.4 , now extends to NVIDIA DGX Station for Windows. CUDA 13.5 also introduces more customization of how GPU work is scheduled via locality domains and NVIDIA Multi-Process Service (MPS). And CUDA 13.5 provides innovations across libraries, compilers, NVIDIA CUDA Tile , and developer tools. This post will showcase the highlights of CUDA 13.5. CUDA 13.5 enhancements Some notable enhancements that come with CUDA 13.5 include: Locality domain enhancements CUDA 13.5 gives applications a choice between uniform streaming multiprocessor (SM) partitions across locality domains or partitions that include all available SMs. By default, localized green-context partitions use the same guaranteed SM count per domain, leaving supplemental SMs outside those partitions. The new cudaDevSmResourceGroupLocalityDomainSupplementalSms flag, combined with cudaDevSmResourceGroupLocalityDomainId , includes these additional SMs within each selected domain. This enables applications to use all device SMs when partitioning across locality domains, although the resulting partitions may differ in size. Applications can use discovery mode in the cudaDevSmResourceSplit() API to obtain each partition’s SM count and distribute work accordingly. This allows you to choose between the uniformity and predictability of uniform SM size for each locality domain, or to choose the maximum number of SMs that each locality domain has, and utilize as much of the GPU hardware as possible. For more info see the CUDA Runtime API . NVIDIA MPS MPS v3 gives you more control over how workloads share a GPU, from scheduling individual servers to assigning resources to groups of clients. Weighted timeslicing Weighted timeslicing lets you give longer compute turns to servers hosting workloads that need them. Set a base timeslice, scale it per MPS server, and independently tune how aggressively the GPU switches between workloads. SM partition load balancing SM partition load balancing lets workloads use capacity beyond their base partition when resources are available. Enable borrowing with --max-chunks , and allow a partition to lend its SMs while it has no attached clients with --shareable=true . These settings are independent, so a partition can borrow, lend, or do both. MPS reclaims borrowed resources before reassigning them, while applications continue to see a stable base partition size. Cgroup-based routing Cgroup-based routing connects your workload launcher’s process groupings to MPS resource policies. Map a cgroup v2 subtree to an MPS namespace, and clients connecting through the daemon’s main socket are routed to that namespace automatically. SM partition assignments Per-namespace SM partition assignments let you choose a partition for each device once, then apply that selection to every client routed to the namespace. You no longer need to configure CUDA_MPS_SM_PARTITION separately for those clients. Namespace assignments take precedence, while devices without an assignment retain the environment-variable fallback. Polling-based fallback for memory accounting Polling-based memory accounting provides a fallback when cgroup threshold notifications are missing or unreliable. During eviction decisions, MPS can read current usage and limits directly instead of relying on cached notification state. To force polling, run nvidia-cuda-mps-control memacct set force_polling=true before memory accounting starts. This adds work per eviction decision but removes its dependence on notification delivery. Batched 1d copies in CUDA graphs CUDA 13.5 adds CUDA Graph support for batched 1D memory copies. Applications can now include existing cudaMemcpyBatchAsync calls in stream capture without changing the batched-copy call syntax, allowing multiple transfers to be captured and replayed as part of a reusable graph workflow. Applications can also add batched-copy nodes explicitly and update compatible copy addresses and sizes without changing the batch structure. Windows driver modes on NVIDIA Rubin Starting with the NVIDIA Rubin architecture, CUDA supports Windows Driver Display Model (WDDM) and Microsoft Compute Driver Model (MCDM), with MCDM providing the compute-only driver model. Tesla Compute Cluster (TCC) is not supported on Rubin and later GPUs. Applications and deployment tools that assume TCC mode should use the supported WDDM or MCDM configuration for their target system. CUDA Tile updates Multi-gpu communication in CUDA Tile CUDA 13.5 adds support for multi-GPU communication directly within CUDA Tile kernels . Unicast pointers let a kernel access memory on another NVLink-connected GPU, while multicast pointers and dedicated multimem operations support reductions and stores across multiple GPUs on NVIDIA NVSwitch fabrics with NVIDIA NVLink SHARP support. Applications prepare the shared-memory mappings before launch, then combine communication with computation inside the kernel, enabling workloads such as fused matrix multiplication and cross-GPU reduction. Tile to single instruction multi-thread (SIMT) interoperability (public preview) CUDA 13.5 allows CUDA Tile kernels to call SIMT library device functions directly. Before this release, Tile and SIMT library code could only be combined across kernel boundaries, with data passing through global memory between them. With this preview, kernels written in cuTile Python or CUDA Tile C++ can call device functions from SIMT libraries in the middle of their own code, on data that is already in registers or shared memory. These libraries include NVIDIA NVSHMEM , NVIDIA CCCL Coop , NVIDIA Warp and NVIDIA MathDx , which covers NVIDIA cuFFTDx, NVIDIA cuBLASDx, NVIDIA cuSolverDx, and NVIDIA nvCOMPDx, and this interop support will be enabled by each of these libraries soon. A tile library (.tilelib) packages interface and implementation information for SIMT library functions. The compiler partitions each tile across threads the way the library expects, communicates any shared memory and synchronization requirements, and produces a single kernel. To enable the preview in C++, compile with nvcc --tile-preview simt and pass the tilelib to the tile compiler. In cuTile Python, use cuda.tile_preview.foreign_call , provided by the cuda.tile_preview package. In 13.5, the Tile-SIMT interop preview covers library functions only. Calling your own __device__ functions from tile code is planned for a future release. For more information, see the documentation . NVIDIA CUDA Python NVIDIA CUDA Python continues to expand Pythonic access to CUDA programming. The CUDA Python core library cuda.core 1.2 introduces batched memory copies, Programmatic Dependent Launch (PDL), simpler runtime compilation, and more flexible CUDA Graph updates. Batched memory copies The new cuda.core.utils.copy_batch() submits multiple buffer copies through a single CUDA driver call. CopyOptions provides control over source access ordering, memory-location hints, and overlap behavior, giving applications more control over data movement. The following example submits two independent copies using existing source and destination buffers: from cuda.core.utils import copy_batch # Each source and destination pair must have matching sizes.
# Copies within the batch must not alias.
copy_batch( stream, srcs=[src_a, src_b], dsts=[dst_a, dst_b],
) stream.sync() PDL from Python LaunchConfig now exposes PDL through the programmatic_stream_serialization option. On GPUs with compute capability 9.

title: How NVIDIA Factory Operations Blueprint Coordinates AI Agents to Investigate Production Issues
abstract: A Siemens report estimates that unplanned downtime costs an average large plant in the surveyed sectors $253 million per year . Whether investigating a failed circuit board or responding to a rush order, factory teams must gather evidence across systems, consult specialists, and coordinate the next step. The data may be available, but turning it into a response takes substantial time and effort. The NVIDIA Factory Operations Blueprint (FOX) provides a reference architecture for adding a factory manager agent to existing factory systems. Developers connect their existing data and tools, configure specialized agents, and define which decisions require operator review. These agents can monitor operations in real time, identify bottlenecks, investigate the root causes of errors or defects, and orchestrate robot fleets to reduce downtime and improve yield. Production planning and inspection are two workflows where factory agents can help teams respond to new orders and product designs. At the Siemens Electronics Factory in Erlangen , which produces more than a thousand products a year, frequent changeovers for new products or orders make both tasks important. For rush orders, agents built with the FOX Blueprint and powered by NVIDIA Nemotron run simulations through Siemens Intelligence Center X. These simulations balance costs, existing orders, supply levels, and line setups—without requiring a planner to manually query each system. The end-to-end agentic system can enable cost savings of up to 20%. For new product designs, Siemens is combining its product lifecycle management software and Process Preparation X with NVIDIA Cosmos and NVIDIA Omniverse to generate a virtual prototype and synthetic training data. This helps electronics manufacturers prepare and optimize automated optical inspection (AOI) processes before physical production begins. This virtual production preparation can reduce time to market by up to 40%. The following super AI agent video includes the Siemens production-planning example from NVIDIA GTC 2026 Berlin. Video 1. This post presents a FOX reference example for a surface-mount technology (SMT) assembly line for printed circuit board (PCB) production. It explains how a factory manager agent connects factory data and coordinates specialized agents to inspect suspected defects, arrange rework, and investigate likely causes. Figure 1. FOX connects agent reasoning with factory knowledge, specialized capabilities, and equipment interfaces Building a factory agent system with FOX The Factory Manager Agent coordinates specialized agents and existing equipment using real-time factory data. Developers adapt the agent’s skills, data connections, knowledge, and tools to their production processes so that it can investigate problems and coordinate a response. Component Blueprint capabilities Developer responsibilities Manager agent Persistent agent environment with skills, tools, memory, and delegation Task definitions, completion criteria, and application integration Factory knowledge Data onboarding and retrieval patterns Mappings for identifiers, timestamps, units, and source permissions Specialist agents Workflow examples for inspection, root cause analysis, reporting, and fleet management Factory-specific criteria, additional specialists, and output validation Equipment integration MCP and API integration patterns; equipment connections through ROS 2 and NVIDIA Isaac Sim Physical equipment connections and handling policies Deployment Profiles for services, model endpoints, and optional simulated cells Resource selection, endpoint configuration, and access boundary checks Table 1. Blueprint capabilities and developer responsibilities for factory agent deployment Factory Manager Agent components FOX shows how to use the NVIDIA Agent Toolkit to build a long-running Factory Manager Agent from three core components: LLM : Interprets tasks, connects data across factory systems, develops plans, and assesses results. Developers can choose a frontier model, such as GPT-6 Astra, or an open model, such as NVIDIA Nemotron, depending on deployment requirements. Agent harness: Connects the manager to tools, skills, persistent memory, and specialist agents. NemoClaw serves as the default harness, with support for alternatives. The harness manages background tasks and scheduled jobs while keeping the manager available to the operator. NVIDIA OpenShell: Isolates the execution environment and enforces access policies for files, commands, and network destinations. Factory policies define permitted actions and when operator review is required. Factory data and specialist agents Developers connect existing machine databases, manufacturing execution systems (MES), and enterprise resource planning (ERP) systems through adapters and mappings. Manuals and operating procedures help the manager interpret the data. An Elasticsearch database stores information for retrieval and retains the investigation context. The manager delegates focused tasks to LLM-based specialist agents, each with its own instructions, context, skills, and tools. Specialists can call models such as NVIDIA Cosmos for visual inspection and Kumo for time-series anomaly detection, then return findings to guide the manager’s next step. Developers can adapt these roles to their own production processes. On-premises deployment FOX can run on an NVIDIA DGX Station with the agent environment, required AI models, and data stores hosted locally. A fully on-premises deployment requires every model and service endpoint to remain within the factory network. This keeps production records, images, prompts, and investigation results local. Developers using an externally hosted model must assess what data is sent to that endpoint. The SMT reference example is separate from the Siemens production-planning implementation. It follows an AOI alert through inspection, rework, and root cause analysis; other factory workflows can use the same architecture with different data, specialists, and equipment connections. Applying FOX to an SMT assembly line PCBs are used in many electronic products. SMT has largely automated their assembly, though some steps remain manual. When a defect is detected at one station, the problem may have originated several steps earlier. An SMT assembly line can include the following stations: Solder paste printer: Applies paste to component pads. Pick-and-place machine: Positions components on the solder paste. Reflow oven: Melts and cools the solder to form mechanical and electrical connections. AOI and in-circuit testing (ICT): Check for visible defects and test electrical characteristics. Board integration: Installs larger components. Standard operating procedure (SOP) station: Handles manual assembly according to standard operating procedures. Functional test: Checks that the board operates as intended. Packaging station: Prepares the board for shipment. Figure 2. The PCB production workflow, from solder paste printing through inspection, testing, and packaging An AOI alert may be a false positive, while a confirmed defect or failed functional test can require rework. For a suspected solder defect, the Factory Manager Agent coordinates a second inspection, arranges handling if needed, and investigates what went wrong. Receiving the AOI alert Developers connect the AOI station through a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server or API that exposes inspection records to the manager’s tools. For the flagged board, the manager retrieves the board identifier, affected component, and inspection image, then requests a secondary assessment. The board identifier connects this request to records from other stations. Adapters preserve identifiers, timestamps, units, and source references so the agents can retrieve the board’s production history and the machine conditions it encountered.

title: Use NVIDIA NeMo to Turn Agent Failures into Tests and Harness Fixes
abstract:
Turn production evidence into prioritized issues and custom evaluations that help you improve prompts, tools, models, memory, skills, and harness code. When you build an agent for your domain , generic benchmark scores may not explain its failures. An agent might choose the wrong tool, follow the wrong workflow branch, miss relevant context, use an unnecessarily expensive model, or complete a task without meeting a domain-specific requirement. Improving an agent requires more than model tuning. Prompts, tools, routing, memory, skills, control flow, and other code all shape production reliability. Traces help you investigate failures, while evaluations help you measure whether a change improves agent behavior. This tutorial walks you through one complete optimization cycle: use NVIDIA NeMo Compass to identify a failure in recorded traces, create an evaluation with NVIDIA NeMo Eval Author, update the agent’s instructions, and compare results on development and held-out tasks. Follow along with the NVIDIA NemoClaw blueprint for agent optimization . The blueprint uses Hermes Agent in an NVIDIA OpenShell sandbox, with recorded traces from a fictional company. The agent harness is the optimization surface One wrong tool call can derail an entire task. The cause may be an unclear tool description, a routing rule, or missing context in the agent harness. A trace helps identify where the run went wrong. Our example agent is a Hermes enterprise assistant for a fictional company, connected through Model Context Protocol (MCP) to the company’s chat, email, files, and tickets. We asked it to “draft a message with project updates.” It drafted the message but also called the send_message tool without user confirmation. Addressing this error requires examining both the harness instructions and tool execution. Prerequisites Use a Linux machine running Docker natively. The recommended configuration is Ubuntu 24.04 with 8 vCPUs and 32 GB of RAM. You also need: OpenShell 0.1.2 and Harbor 0.22.0 An NVIDIA API key from build.nvidia.com A coding agent that NeMo Eval Author supports, such as Codex or Claude Code Follow the full step-by-step tutorial on GitHub or get started with an NVIDIA Brev launchable . NeMo Compass: Find what to fix first The NemoClaw blueprint for agent optimization uses three libraries: NeMo Compass, NeMo Eval Author, and NVIDIA NeMo Relay. NeMo Compass analyzes stored agent traces and evaluation evidence to find recurring problems, identify evaluation gaps, and prioritize improvements. Rather than requiring you to inspect each run, NeMo Compass reduces a large trace corpus to a structured backlog of issues, supporting examples, and recommended areas for improvement or experimentation. Each Hermes run in the example is recorded as one JSON trace per line. We pointed NeMo Compass at the 42 traces in the repository, along with ETHOS.md , a short file that defines the assistant’s expected behavior. compass --config configs/trace-analyst.yaml \
--trace.filesystem.path traces/world-v3/production/insights.jsonl NeMo Compass returns findings based on multiple signals: Signs of unusual behavior How the agent uses tools Divergence from the agent’s intended behavior NeMo Compass also provides trace IDs that link each signal to the relevant agent runs. These trace IDs support the overall finding. In these runs, the agent sent messages without user confirmation. NeMo Compass identified this error by comparing the agent’s actions with the rules in ETHOS.md . In our internal benchmarks, running the full set of NeMo Compass signals against a dataset of thousands of traces identified anomalies that a coding agent assigned a similar task missed. Build evaluations around real agent work with NeMo Eval Author After finding an issue with NeMo Compass, create a test that reproduces the problem. NeMo Eval Author provides coding agent skills and workflows to help you create these tests. NeMo Eval Author supports two agent evaluation formats: Harbor evaluations and NVIDIA NeMo Gym evaluations . Install NeMo Eval Author’s skills in your coding agent and instruct it to use them. Provide the NeMo Compass findings, raw traces, the agent’s ETHOS.md file, and access to your agent repository as context. The evaluations should measure agent behavior relevant to your agent’s requirements. Review and tune the generated evaluations to make sure they reflect those requirements. In our example, the coding agent created four Harbor evaluations with tasks similar to “draft a response.” NeMo Eval Author also creates verifiers that determine whether an agent meets specific criteria. In this example, the verifier checks whether the agent called the send_message tool without human confirmation and marks that run as a failure. NeMo Eval Author can help you create custom evaluations before production data exists, using agent requirements from ETHOS.md and code details such as tool definitions and existing workflows. As real traces and known failures become available, use NeMo Eval Author to expand your evaluation suite, so it continues to reflect how your agent is used. Change one part of the harness After identifying an issue and writing tests for it, update the harness. In our example, we changed the Hermes agent’s SOUL.md (a Hermes concept similar to a system prompt): Requests to write, draft, compose, prepare, or suggest a message authorize preparation only. Provide the draft for review and stop before sending it. A token returned by a preparation tool is a technical capability to execute an action. It does not establish the user's consent to that action. Harness changes can range from simple fixes like this to more complex middleware implementations, plugin extensions, and other agent harness patterns . Provide the coding agent with the NeMo Compass outputs, your agent’s ETHOS.md file, and your agent implementation. This context grounds the coding agent’s proposal. Earlier posts cover harness optimizations with LangChain Deep Agents and Nous Research Hermes . Measure before and after After updating the agent, we reran the evaluation tasks created by NeMo Eval Author. Two tasks, labeled “Held out,” were withheld from the coding agents proposing harness changes. These held-out tasks help assess whether the changes generalize beyond the development tasks. Evaluation set Baseline passes/runs Updated-agent passes/runs Tool calls, before/after Development, 2 tasks x 3 runs 3/6 6/6 10 to 6 Held out, 2 tasks x 3 runs 4/6 6/6 28 to 15 Table 1. Evaluation results before and after the harness change In our example, we started with a small set of evaluation tasks focused narrowly on the NeMo Compass findings. For your production agent, build an evaluation suite that covers a broad range of behaviors. In our experience, production suites often contain hundreds to a few thousand examples. Accept changes only when they improve both the test cases and the held-out set. If results are inconclusive, or a change fixes one problem but introduces a regression, run NeMo Compass on the new traces from the proposed agent. The coding agent can use these new insights to refine the change. As you iterate on this process, ensure that the held-out cases remain hidden from the coding agent to avoid overfitting. Run the loop again After a successful harness change, repeat the analysis to identify the next issue. We ran NeMo Compass on the updated agent’s scored traces, and it no longer reported the sending-without-confirmation finding. It identified another issue: for some queries, the agent found the answer but failed to ground its response in the retrieved evidence. That finding is the focus of the next round of testing and fixes. Apply the optimization loop to an engineering agent The same trace-to-evaluation loop can be applied to agents that perform more complex technical tasks. In an engineering workflow, evaluations need to measure engineering outcomes as well as the efficiency of the agent’s tool use.

title: Use decision models with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Evaluations
abstract: Some of the questions you ask when evaluating an agent are narrow and repeatable. Did this response stay on policy? Is this tool call safe to approve? Does this answer match the retrieved context? Decision models answer exactly that kind of question. They take a structured state and a fixed set of allowed answers and return a calibrated probability over them, rather than free-form text whose confidence drifts from run to run. That makes them a strong fit for the scoring step in an agent evaluation, where you want a label and a number you can threshold and trust. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Evaluations , a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, scores an agent through its entire lifecycle, on demand during development, in batch jobs against stored sessions, and online against production traffic. Alongside 15 built-in evaluators, AgentCore Evaluations supports custom evaluators that you define as either an LLM-as-a-judge or a code-based evaluator. Custom LLM-as-a-judge evaluators apply your instructions and rating scale with a model in Amazon Bedrock. Code-based evaluators run your own logic in an AWS Lambda function, and that logic can call your choice of external system, model, or API, including a decision model. Decision models suit questions with a fixed set of answers that an informed person could decide at a glance, such as whether the agent refused a request or whether a response stayed on topic. After you validate a question on your own traffic, a decision model can be sufficient for that decision or score, and you can extend the same approach to specific harmfulness or stereotyping categories in your policy. Because both backends can answer several questions about the same state in a single request, you can use them as a screening layer rather than a replacement, running a pass or fail signal across your metrics to select the turns that warrant deeper assessment by the built-in evaluators, whose explanations help you investigate what went wrong. This post shows how to connect two decision model backends to AgentCore Evaluations through code-based evaluators. The first is Jev , a hosted decision model from TypeSafe. The second is Strands Decider 2B , an open-source decision model you run yourself. By the end of this post, you will know how to convert the AgentCore evaluator input into a decision model request, and the model’s probabilities back into an AgentCore evaluation result. First, though, when should you reach for a custom LLM-as-a-judge evaluator, and when does a decision model fit better? The next section breaks down what a decision model is and the trade-offs involved. A decision model is a small, specialized model trained to select from a fixed set of options and return calibrated confidence scores rather than generating free-form text. A general-purpose large language model (LLM) evaluator produces a score with a rationale. A decision model instead produces a probability distribution over predefined answers. That gives you a direct confidence measure you can threshold, aggregate, and act on programmatically. This makes decision models well-suited for evaluation tasks where the judgment can be stated as a choice among a fixed set of options: “Is this response grounded?” or “Did the agent complete the user’s goal?” Decision models are most useful when you want a well-calibrated confidence score alongside the label, not just a binary judgment. They are also appropriate when you want to enforce a specific rubric consistently without relying on a general-purpose LLM to interpret it. Jev, the hosted decision model from TypeSafe, and Strands Decider , an open-source, 2-billion-parameter decision model from the Strands Agents team, both support three types of questions. A noul question poses a yes/no question and returns a probability between 0 (no) and 1 (yes). A choice question asks which of up to 255 options applies, returning the most probable option along with the full distribution and a confidence. A score question asks which of 2 to 10 ordered levels applies, returning a probability-weighted score, the distribution over levels, and a confidence. Many evaluation rubrics fit one of these types. “Is every fact in this response supported by the tool results?” is a yes/no question, and “How helpful was this response, on a four-level rubric?” is a score. The built-in evaluators in AgentCore today use a general-purpose LLM to assess the agent response against a rubric and explain its judgment. This is valuable when the evaluation requires connecting evidence, identifying missing information, or working through a response in depth in tasks where the explanation is as useful as the score. Decision models are not a replacement for LLM evaluators. They’re an addition that the code-based evaluator framework makes possible. Use them for narrow, well-defined checks alongside the built-in evaluators’ broader assessment. To show how these evaluator types work together, this post builds an end-to-end example of an HR Assistant agent evaluated by deterministic code-based checks, built-in LLM-as-a-judge evaluators, and decision-model evaluators backed by Jev or Strands Decider 2B. The agent is built with Strands Agents and deployed to AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. It answers employee questions using five tools that return fixed mock data such as paid time off (PTO) balances, PTO requests, HR policies, benefits, and pay stubs. We use fixed data in this code sample to make it straightforward to verify evaluator behavior from LLM-as-a-judge and decision models. When you additionally have ground truth, you can confirm whether each evaluator catches the right failures. This code sample helps you set up the framework for testing decision models compared to LLM-as-a-judge for your own use cases. Figure 1: End-to-end architecture of the HR Assistant evaluated by code-based checks, built-in evaluators, and decision-model evaluators backed by Jev or Strands Decider To deploy the sample, you need the following: You can find the full code sample in the AgentCore samples GitHub repository . Two Python scripts handle everything: Running evaluate.py without flags executes five steps: At this point you have a working evaluation pipeline with deterministic checks and LLM-as-a-judge scoring. Decision-model evaluators are opt-in. You can add them with a flag, and they run alongside the base evaluators with no changes to the existing flow. Using the flags --with-jev --jev-secret-arn <ARN> deploys jev-evaluator and registers three evaluators: JevGroundedness , JevHelpfulness , and JevGoalCompletion . Using the flag --with-decider deploys strands-decider-evaluator and registers the same three evaluators backed by Strands Decider 2B. Add --decider-ec2 to auto-provision the Amazon EC2 instance, security groups, IAM role, and Lambda VPC configuration without manual console steps. Figure 2: The evaluation pipeline deployed by evaluate.py, from deterministic checks through built-in and decision-model evaluators Each decision-model backend contributes three evaluators: Using the flags --with-jev and --with-decider creates a custom code-based evaluator, where you have complete control of the code you want to run as your evaluator. We create AWS Lambda functions where the decision model is invoked inside an AWS Lambda function and returns a label or a numeric value. This Lambda function is registered as the code-based evaluator in AgentCore Evaluations. The Lambda that is registered as the evaluator receives OpenTelemetry spans of the agent. The spans.py module normalizes the shapes OpenTelemetry content can arrive in and then formats it appropriately to make the call to the decision model. For trace-level evaluation, only the targeted turn and brief prior history are sent, whereas the full conversation is included for session-level.

title: Smart Approvals in Amazon Quick: Human oversight where it matters
abstract: How should security leaders preserve human oversight as AI agents take on more work? Permissions establish which actions agents can take, but a permitted action can still warrant a person’s judgment. Requiring approval for every step might seem like the safest approach, yet multi-step tasks can produce repeated prompts , even for routine actions. Research on security warnings shows that attention and adherence can decline with repetition. The challenge isn’t to require more approvals, but to preserve attention for decisions that need human review. Smart Approvals in Amazon Quick addresses this challenge by reviewing eligible actions within your existing controls. It evaluates each proposed action against the user’s request and either approves it automatically or returns it to the user for review. It does this without granting additional permissions or removing required human approvals. Security leaders retain control over which actions must always go to a person, while Smart Approvals is designed to reduce unnecessary interruptions in routine work. Figure 1: Policy determines eligibility. Smart Approvals approves eligible actions or returns them to the user for review. Policy denials remain blocked Quick evaluates each proposed action against Custom Permissions, Quick Guardrails, connector action permissions, and the user’s settings before automated review. Denied actions remain denied, and mandatory human approvals still apply. With Smart Approvals enabled, an action is eligible only when the user’s setting is “Ask each time” and no other control requires human approval. Connector action permissions, configured when a connector is created, can require human approval for specific actions. Administrators use Custom Permissions to determine who can use Smart Approvals. It’s on by default, but profiles with deny-by-default enabled must explicitly allow it. Users can also turn Smart Approvals off for themselves. That choice applies across conversations and scheduled runs. When it’s off, actions otherwise eligible for automated review require the user’s approval, and no account-level setting can turn it back on for them. Smart Approvals uses a separate model, the classifier, to evaluate eligible actions against the user’s request and a bounded view of the conversation. It considers what the action does, where data goes, and who it affects. It can consult the user’s knowledge graph, which contains people and working relationships drawn from connected sources. This helps it understand how recipients relate to the user, such as whether a recipient is in the user’s reporting chain. This lookup stays within your Quick account. Quick doesn’t use the content the classifier reviews, including knowledge graph data, to train models or improve the service. An action can match the request and still warrant human review. Examples include sending content outside the organization or to senior leaders in the user’s reporting chain, changing access, deleting records, or initiating payments. This list isn’t complete, and the classifier also weighs the surrounding context. Reviewing actions against the user’s request adds a check against indirect prompt injection, where instructions in retrieved content attempt to redirect the agent. Quick instructs both the agent and classifier to treat that content as information, not instructions. Model review can still make mistakes, so actions that must always receive human approval, including those that move sensitive data, should require it through connector action permissions. The classifier provides judgment. The permission service enforces authority. Each automatic approval is single-use, applies only to the exact action and parameters reviewed, and grants no ongoing permission. Quick labels automatic approvals in the conversation. Actions the classifier doesn’t approve return to the user, as do timeouts and other review failures, which never grant automatic approval. These enforcement boundaries limit what an approval authorizes. They don’t establish that the classifier’s judgment was correct. An account manager asks Quick to prepare a quarterly business review brief for AnyCompany using her team’s account notes and last quarter’s email. She then asks Quick to send it to two colleagues she names. Assuming the send is eligible for automated review, Smart Approvals evaluates the proposed action against her request and the available conversation context. Now suppose an account note says the brief should also go to an all-sales distribution list of about 2,000 people. That would change the audience beyond the recipients she specified, so Smart Approvals is designed to return the proposed send to her for review, where she can decline it. An approval to send to the original recipients can’t be reused for the wider audience. The Quick permission service records permission updates associated with Smart Approvals in AWS CloudTrail in your account. Each event identifies the user, connector, action, and time, and marks the request as associated with Smart Approvals. That marker doesn’t establish that the permission service accepted the grant or that the action ran. Quick also records permission-check verdicts, including denials from connector action permissions, and changes to a user’s Smart Approvals setting. Investigators can correlate these events by user and time with other Quick activity in CloudTrail and logs delivered through Amazon CloudWatch Logs . Chat logs capture the user’s request, system response, and conversation context. Agent metadata logs record changes to agents. Records from the destination system, such as a sent email or updated ticket, confirm whether the action completed. Together, these sources help reconstruct what happened without treating approval as proof of execution. CloudTrail Event history retains events for 90 days, so configure a trail for longer investigations. Because chat logs can contain sensitive content, restrict access and consider CloudWatch Logs data protection policies to mask sensitive data. Because Smart Approvals is on by default, begin by confirming that actions requiring human approval are configured through connector action permissions. Set up a CloudTrail trail and delivery of chat logs and agent metadata logs to CloudWatch Logs to support investigations. Chat logs capture only activity after delivery is configured, so earlier approvals will lack that conversation context. With approval requirements and logging in place, use Custom Permissions to limit Smart Approvals to a pilot team working on a defined workflow before extending it to other teams. Before the pilot, define what success looks like: fewer prompts for routine actions, with consequential actions still returning to a person for review. During the pilot, review a sample of automatic approvals and test high-impact cases, such as sending content outside the organization or adding a recipient introduced by a document. Confirm that these cases come back to the user. Confirm that your team can trace each action from approval through execution. Expand to more teams and workflows only when the results meet those criteria, and reassess as actions and policies change. The measure of effective oversight isn’t how often an agent asks for approval, but whether people retain control over consequential decisions. For security leaders, the case for expanding Smart Approvals should rest on evidence from the pilot. Fewer prompts are valuable when they preserve attention without weakening accountability. For setup steps, see Smart Approvals in the governance section of the Amazon Quick User Guide.

title: Four layers of context engineering for production AI agents: How Deep Insight applies them in working code
abstract: When production AI agents handle tasks such as data analysis and report generation, context management can become a major bottleneck. A 200K-token window sounds generous until a real-world task burns through most of it in minutes. Data analysis and report generation leave the agent failing mid-execution, losing accuracy, or driving up costs. A body of published guidance already addresses this, but the individual techniques are easier to read about than to apply. Applied together, they make a measurable difference: in the reference implementation this post walks through, a single write-and-execute tool cuts the tokens each script adds to context by about 95 percent, and loading skills on demand shrinks the system prompt by about 97 percent. This series organizes that guidance into practices you can apply directly. Anthropic’s engineering posts, together with features built into the Strands Agents SDK, converge on four layers of context engineering: isolate context at the architecture level, control it through prompts, externalize it to the filesystem, and verify it with independent agents and safeguards. In this post (Part 2), you will learn how each layer works and what it looks like in working code. We applied these techniques in Deep Insight , an open source multi-agent data analysis solution built on the Strands Agents SDK and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, which serves as the reference implementation throughout. The first post defined five core challenges that production multi-agent systems must solve. It introduced how Strands Agents SDK , Amazon Bedrock and Bedrock AgentCore , and AWS Fargate each address different layers of the problem, with code examples. This second post takes the four layers of context engineering practice that sit on top of that architecture and shows each one implemented. The third post guides you through deploying and operating agents in a secure private network on Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC), covering everything needed for real-world operations. Context engineering is the discipline of optimizing the information in a large language model (LLM)’s limited context window so agents perform at their best. Anthropic Claude Sonnet 4.5, available on Amazon Bedrock, offers a 200K context window, but complex production tasks quickly exceed it. For example, a seemingly straightforward request like “ Analyze sales data and create a DOCX report ” runs through several stages: data loading and exploration (5 min), category-based sales analysis (3 min), generating five charts for time-series analysis (10 min), statistical validation (3 min), and final report generation (5 min). Together they consume over 150K tokens across 15 minutes. Processing such tasks in a single context causes problems: the window overflows mid-task, stale context degrades performance, and errors require re-running the whole pipeline. As context grows, attention to important information drops, and inefficiency raises cost under per-token pricing. “As the number of tokens in the context window increases, the model’s ability to accurately recall information from that context decreases (Context rot).” — Anthropic, “ Effective Context Engineering for AI Agents ” (2025.09) Context engineering solves exactly these problems, and it is not only a collection of techniques. Spanning architecture design, prompt writing, tool implementation, and verification, it’s a layered discipline where each layer compensates for what the previous ones miss. This post details the four-layer approach you can apply to manage context efficiently. Anthropic has published several techniques for handling long-horizon tasks. Deep Insight groups these techniques into four layers, with each layer addressing the limitations of the others. The following table sets out the four layers. The sections that follow take each layer in order, stating what the layer prescribes, why the preceding layers alone are insufficient, and how the practice is implemented in Deep Insight. Give each specialized agent its own context window and pass only compressed results to the orchestrator. Deep Insight does this with a hierarchy of Coordinator, Planner, Plan Reviewer, Supervisor, and Tool Agents (Coder, Validator, Reporter, Tracker, Auditor). With a single agent, all information, from user requests through data exploration, analysis, chart generation, validation, and reporting, accumulates in one context and easily exceeds the window. Giving each agent its own context keeps even the Coder, which uses the most, under 25K tokens total. Each agent receives only what it needs and signals others with a completion notice and brief summary. The key to isolation is minimizing shared information. Deep Insight uses a Python dictionary, shared_state , that stores only four things: The clues use a fixed CLUES_FORMAT: instead of each agent’s full conversation (tens of thousands of tokens), only compressed core results are passed. This pattern is the one recommended in Anthropic’s “ How We Built Our Multi-Agent Research System ” post, which describes an orchestrator-worker pattern in which a lead agent delegates to specialized subagents, with each agent working only within its own context. You do not need to build it yourself: the agents-as-tools pattern in the Strands Agents SDK provides this isolation at the framework level. Layer 1 isolation alone is not sufficient: even with independent contexts, an agent that generates long responses inflates the Supervisor’s context. Layer 2 limits each agent’s output through prompts. For Deep Insight, we use prompts to limit how much information each agent returns to the Supervisor. Three rules do most of the work, as Deep Insight’s prompts show. “Start with the strongest model and a simple prompt. Then incrementally add specific instructions based on actually observed failure cases.” — Anthropic, “Effective Context Engineering for AI Agents” (2025.09) Each agent’s prompt specifies a maximum response token count, preventing long responses that pollute the Supervisor’s context. Anthropic’s ” Writing Effective Tools for Agents ” post suggests giving tools a CONCISE or DETAILED response option for context efficiency. Apply the same idea one level up, in each agent’s system prompt. In Deep Insight, all agents share one standardized format: The Coder agent’s prompt explicitly states “variables do not persist between scripts.” Every script must include all necessary imports and load data directly. The prompt provides both incorrect and correct examples: The reason this rule relates to context engineering is that referencing variables from previous scripts requires the agent to “remember” prior conversations, which means past code must remain in context. The self-contained principle means past code can be safely removed from context. The Supervisor’s prompt includes the rule “Do not move to the next agent until all checklist items in the current agent’s section are marked [x] .” We express this rule in the prompt because deciding whether the Coder’s work is complete requires the Supervisor to interpret the plan using information from the Tracker’s updates. This judgment is difficult to express in code alone. Layer 1 isolates context between agents, and Layer 2 limits output within agents. But when the Coder agent generates 100 lines of Python code, that code itself enters the context. Even with “respond briefly” prompt instructions, some code can’t be written briefly. Layer 3 uses tool design to move heavy content outside the context, into the filesystem. Four techniques carry most of the benefit, as the following implementation details show. The Coder reads the analysis plan, writes Python, and executes it to generate visualizations. But when the code gets long, the conventional approach (separate file-write and execute tools) adds 100 lines directly to context per script, accumulating over 1,000 lines.

title: How Indegene is modernizing and scaling enterprise data quality in life sciences
abstract: This post is co-written with Shravan K S from Indegene Limited. Enterprise AI is creating new opportunities for life sciences organizations to improve decision-making across commercial, medical, market access, and other business functions. But the quality of every AI model, dashboard, and business insight depends on one thing: trusted data. As enterprise data grows across multiple platforms, pipelines, and business domains, maintaining consistent data quality has become increasingly difficult. Manual data quality rule creation, fragmented governance, and evolving business definitions make it challenging to scale data quality across the enterprise. This post explores how Indegene built a production-grade, large language model (LLM) powered Data Quality Agent within its NEXT Unified Data Platform (NEXT UDP) on AWS. The agent generates context-aware data quality rules, validates them, and produces ready-to-run SQL and Python code under centralized, human-in-the-loop governance. Together, these capabilities help organizations improve data quality at enterprise scale while reducing the effort required to build and maintain data quality programs. Indegene Limited (BSE: 544172, NSE: INDGN) is the strategic operating partner to the life sciences industry, orchestrating commercial, medical, R&D, and safety operations across the product lifecycle. Trusted by the world’s top 20 biopharma companies, Indegene helps run complex, highly regulated workflows at global scale. Indegene combines deep life sciences expertise with AI-embedded platforms and governed operating models to improve speed, consistency, and compliance across mission-critical operations. By integrating technology into how work is executed and scaled, Indegene helps life sciences organizations deliver measurable outcomes in regulated environments. Most organizations have established data quality processes but keeping them effective is becoming increasingly difficult as enterprise data ecosystems evolve. One of the biggest challenges is the divide between technical and business rule ownership. Data engineers typically define technical rules that confirm whether data is structurally correct. For example, verifying that an HCP ID (Healthcare Professional ID) isn’t null, follows the required format, is unique, and maps to a valid reference record. Business teams define rules that determine whether the data makes sense in its operational context. For example, confirming that product market share totals 100 percent within a territory or that an HCP’s prescription activity aligns with their specialty and eligibility criteria. Because technical rules are often maintained in code while business rules reside in glossaries, SOPs, and subject-matter expertise, keeping them aligned and consistently governed across datasets and platforms becomes difficult. Traditional validation techniques also have inherent limitations. Checks for null values, data types, uniqueness, or referential integrity remain essential, but they can’t capture business-specific context. Validating product hierarchies, customer segmentation, territory alignment, or commercial business rules requires domain knowledge that static validation logic can’t easily represent. Creating and maintaining data quality rules is equally demanding. Every new dataset requires data profiling, rule definition, SQL development, validation, and ongoing maintenance. These rules are often spread across SQL scripts, pipeline code, spreadsheets, data catalogs, and tool-specific configurations. As schemas, business definitions, or validation thresholds change, the effort required to update and govern these rules grows significantly. Additionally, the operational impact is significant. Onboarding new datasets becomes slower because many activities are repeated manually. Maintaining quality rules across hundreds of datasets consumes valuable engineering effort. Business users lose confidence when validation rules are difficult to understand, trace, or relate to business context. As a result, data quality often becomes a periodic governance activity rather than a continuous, scalable capability. Traditional data quality tools often operate as standalone capabilities, disconnected from the broader enterprise data ecosystem. As organizations scale AI and analytics, data quality needs to be embedded within the data platform itself, where governance, metadata, lineage, and analytics work together. Indegene addresses this through the NEXT Unified Data Platform (NEXT UDP) , a modern, AI-driven data platform built specifically for life sciences. NEXT UDP brings together fragmented commercial, medical, clinical, and enterprise data into a single, governed environment so organizations can manage the complete data lifecycle from ingestion to analytics. NEXT UDP provides several standalone AI agents, such as the Data Ingestion agent, Data Quality agent, Orchestration agent, Data Catalog agent, and SQL Bot Generator agent. You can use them standalone within your data pipelines or customize them further for agent-to-agent communication. By integrating data ingestion, transformation, data quality, governance, metadata management, and analytics within a unified platform, NEXT UDP helps organizations: Figure 1: NEXT Unified Data Platform dashboard with use cases and AI agents Figure 2: NEXT UDP technical architecture on AWS Indegene’s life sciences clients needed an agent that could run reliably in production and meet strict governance requirements, while giving the team flexibility in how they build it. Within NEXT UDP, Generative AI powers an intelligent Data Quality Agent that augments existing data quality processes. The agent boosts data engineer and data steward productivity by accelerating rule creation, simplifying validation, and helping maintain consistent governance at enterprise scale. Indegene built the Data Quality Agent on a set of AWS services, with Amazon Bedrock, Strands Agents and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore at its core. Amazon Bedrock , provides a choice of foundation models (FMs), built on a foundation of security, privacy, and responsible AI controls . For life sciences organizations, this matters because their data often includes sensitive healthcare professional and patient information. Strands Agents streamlines building and updating the agent, and its evaluation tools help Indegene test rule accuracy, which is critical in regulated life sciences environments. The agent runs on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore , a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. The solution also inherits existing AWS security and audit controls, so Indegene can focus on data quality logic instead of agent infrastructure. Any data quality tool can check for null values, duplicates, or invalid data types. Services such as AWS Glue Data Quality, a capability of AWS Glue, already recommend rules like these from data statistics, and they remain a strong foundation. The harder problem is determining whether the data makes sense for its business purpose. To address this, the Data Quality Agent uses two complementary knowledge bases that combine curated domain knowledge with experience gained from governed usage. The first is an Internal Enterprise knowledge base: It combines internal business glossaries, data dictionaries, SOPs, regulatory guidance, approved data quality rules, validated scripts, profiling results, historical anomalies, and subject matter expert (SME) feedback. Content is ingested, vectorized, and retrieved through Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) to generate data quality rules grounded in enterprise standards and proven outcomes. The second is an External Reference knowledge base: It’s built and periodically updated using approved standardized data quality frameworks, web search, and controlled web-scraping.

title: How U Mobile built agentic telco operations with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
abstract: U Mobile, Malaysia’s newest 5G network provider, has always run its telco operations lean, doing more with less through continuous automation. When new AI capabilities became available, U Mobile explored how to enhance operational efficiency beyond basic productivity gains. The real opportunity was further upstream, in how operations teams diagnose and resolve problems in the first place. The same lean operating discipline shaped the foundation for AiDaH: not a one-off technology initiative, but the next step in a long-running journey to simplify operations and scale capability without adding complexity. When a subscriber can’t purchase a data add-on, resolving it isn’t a single problem. It’s a coordination problem. A customer service agent needs to pull interface logs for error codes. The same agent must then query business support system APIs for subscriber eligibility, and cross-reference internal knowledge bases for applicable business policies. All of that happens across multiple systems, before drafting a single word of response. And when that fails, the ticket escalates to backend IT teams and the subscriber waits even longer. Traditional automation tools can help agents write better responses. What they can’t do is navigate multiple systems, analyze the results, and propose corrective action. Closing that gap takes an agentic architecture built on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. U Mobile’s Information Systems Division (ISD) built exactly that. Working with AWS and AWS Partner Axrail, they created AiDaH, the AI-Driven Agentic Helpdesk, on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. Two capabilities decided the choice. The managed agent runtime meant there was no agent infrastructure to operate. Built-in memory carried conversational context across turns without standing up a separate state store. Within a year of starting the journey, AiDaH handles over 150 documented operational scenarios across six business divisions. U Mobile’s internal measurements show trouble ticket volumes falling by up to 84.5 percent in key categories. In this post, we walk through the six-layer architecture behind AiDaH. We then describe the security foundation beneath the platform, and close with a brief note on the spec-driven method the team used to build it. U Mobile’s IT landscape reflects the complexity typical of modern telecommunications: business support and customer relationship management systems, mobile number portability platforms, big data analytics, and infrastructure monitoring tools, running hybrid across on-premises and cloud. Before AiDaH, this fragmentation meant that even routine diagnoses required manually checking logs, querying subscriber eligibility, and consulting knowledge bases for business policies, across separate systems and portals. Each lookup was a context switch, each context switch was time lost, and each unresolved query became an escalation to a backend IT team. Expanding coverage to additional operational domains compounded the problem, because every new system typically required a bespoke integration. The ISD team’s strategy rested on three pillars. AiDaH started with a principle: think big, start small. U Mobile began conceptualization in late 2025 with two pilot agents and Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases, a fully managed Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) capability. A Q1 2026 pilot brought the internal IT helpdesk online with 4 agents and 20 operational scenarios. Through 2026 the platform hardened and expanded, adding three-tier routing and reaching 6 agents by mid-year. AiDaH went live to 50 L2 call center and branch users in Q3 2026 with 8 agents, and now covers more than 150 documented operational scenarios. The difference between traditional AI assistance and agentic AI is best illustrated through a real example. With a traditional AI assistant, a support agent handling “mobile data not working overseas” gets help drafting a response and some suggested troubleshooting steps, but still manually checks roaming status, verifies eligibility, raises tickets, and sends the final reply. With AiDaH, the system independently checks the subscriber’s roaming configuration, verifies international data eligibility, and identifies the specific point of failure. It then assembles a remediation plan: which services to reset, what configuration to push, and whether a network ticket is warranted. The support agent reviews and confirms, and the actions execute. The investigation that used to consume the agent’s time now happens before they read the first line. The human decision point is preserved where it matters: at the moment something changes on a live subscriber account. In one production case, a subscriber reported being unable to purchase an add-on. AiDaH traced the failure to an error code, “Subscriber has pending order.” It also revealed that the customer had attempted the same purchase more than 30 times across multiple channels over three days, every attempt blocked by the same underlying pending order. AiDaH surfaced the root cause and the remediation steps in a single response. Previously that would have required manual investigation across several systems. AiDaH runs on a layered architecture built on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, deployed in the Asia Pacific (Singapore) Region. Staff interact through Microsoft Teams, a deliberate choice to meet most users where they already work, with no new application to learn and no portal switching. The following diagram shows how the layers fit together. Figure 1: AiDaH’s layered architecture As shown in Figure 1, the platform is organized into six layers. Staff reach AiDaH through Microsoft Teams and a web portal served by Amazon CloudFront and protected by AWS WAF, with an AWS Lambda backend and a REST API for programmatic triggers. The routing brain on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. Every request passes a pre-flight security check covering role-based access control, identity validation, and guardrails, then enters a cost-optimized routing tier. Roughly 70 percent of requests resolve through deterministic keyword matching with no model invocation, 20 percent are classified by a lightweight model, and only 10 percent require the full orchestrator. The cheapest path that can confidently handle the request is the one that runs. Eight experts spanning customer relationship management, customer problem management, number portability, order and SIM operations, infrastructure monitoring, big data analytics, cloud cost management, and finance operations. They communicate over the Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol, which lets them delegate subtasks and complete cross-system workflows no single agent could handle alone. Layer 4: Gateways and backend APIs AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, exposes U Mobile’s backends to agents through a unified Model Context Protocol (MCP) interface. Behind each gateway sit AWS Lambda functions and MCP servers that translate agent intent into calls against a specific system. Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases, the fully managed RAG capability, grounds agent responses in governed content, using an Amazon OpenSearch Serverless vector store. Content spans a shared enterprise knowledge base and a separate finance corpus. AgentCore memory, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, maintains conversational context across turns, and Amazon DynamoDB holds the six-tier role-based access control model and session metadata. U Mobile’s on-premises and cloud operational systems are reached over AWS Transit Gateway and AWS Site-to-Site VPN, an IPsec-encrypted tunnel with no public internet exposure. Tracing a single request makes the interaction between the layers concrete. Consider a support agent who types a port-in status question into the AiDaH channel in Microsoft Teams. Onboarding a new operational domain adds a gateway and its MCP tool definitions at step 5.

title: How big is the open model economy today?
abstract: My longest running agent testbed has been building the Interconnects Dashboard — an aggregator of all of the best data on open model adoption and performance from across the web. This dashboard is freely available and becoming quite useful. Still, all the measurements we have on open model adoption are incredibly imprecise. We have noisy platform metrics, marketing-related metrics from startups, and imperfect public evaluations. It takes an informed eye to figure out where things are going. These research notes are my current best approximations of where we stand. As with most things on Interconnects, our goal is to build well more value than we capture, so the data on the dashboard will remain free for the foreseeable future. These notes will be more raw than many of my articles, a place for sharing what I’m mulling over but don’t have complete evidence for (yet). They will be primarily paid, enabling me to speak more freely. If you work in AI policy or policy-facing research, please reach out to us and we can likely get discounted or free access. The primary question I wanted to address today is: What is the market for open model inference? Is it growing? Is it a rounding error relative to OpenAI/Anthropic? I’ve been building the best measurements I can here, primarily using the open model inference startups Baseten, Fireworks, and Together AI as the bellwethers here (along with the open model share of OpenRouter’s token volume, which they thankfully report in their API). The hyperscalers also likely have a major footprint here, e.g. Amazon Bedrock and Azure’s model garden, but I haven’t seen them break down usage by model category. The startups’ fates are much more directly correlated with the success of open model inference as a category. For the latest data, we can start with a slide from my talk on the open model economy (recording here ). These are the public disclosures from the open model startups on their token volume, over time, log-scale. This shows near-exponential growth, before the uptick that would follow GLM 5.2’s step change in open agents . For example, Fireworks announced at their first company conference this week that they’re serving more than 40T tokens per day to customers’ customized models. This is just one slice of their inference, a vertical that they said grew over 2x from this summer, so I would expect their total number this fall to be well above 100T tokens when we get the next update. My first instinct with these numbers has been to ground them versus any closed model or hyperscale company we can, at least in terms of token volume. Thankfully, Google releases token volumes for the entire platform and API usage in their earnings reports.
