title: martin-olivier/airgorah
abstract:
Airgorah A WiFi security auditing software Installation | Usage | Credits Airgorah is a WiFi security auditing software that can capture nearby WiFi traffic, discover clients connected to access points, perform deauthentication attacks, capture handshakes and PMKIDs, and crack the password of access points. It is written in Rust and uses GTK4 for the graphical part. ⭐ Don't forget to put a star if you like the project! Legal ⚠️ Airgorah is designed to be used in testing and discovering flaws in networks you are owner of. Performing attacks on WiFi networks you are not owner of is illegal in almost all countries. I am not responsible for whatever damage you may cause by using this software. Requirements This software only works on linux . The graphical interface runs as a normal
user (so it works under both X11 and Wayland ). When a privileged operation is
needed, it launches a small privileged agent ( airgorah-agent ) via polkit ,
which will prompt for authentication once. You will also need a wireless network card that supports monitor mode and packet injection . Installation The installation instructions are available here . Usage The documentation about the usage of the application is available here . License This project is released under MIT license. Contributing If you have any question about the usage of the application, do not hesitate to open a discussion If you want to report a bug or provide a feature, do not hesitate to open an issue or submit a pull request

title: Postman silently auto-installs AI plugins and attempts to share all API data
abstract:
[SEVERE] Desktop auto-installs Codex/Claude plugins; installer attempts to trust its own startup hook #14370 New issue Copy link New issue Copy link Open Open [SEVERE] Desktop auto-installs Codex/Claude plugins; installer attempts to trust its own startup hook #14370 Copy link Description indicava opened on Oct 25, 2026 Issue body actions Is there an existing issue for this? I have searched the tracker for existing similar issues and I know that duplicates will be closed Describe the Issue Opening Postman on my Mac was followed by unexpected changes to my coding agents: recurring MCP authentication warnings and Codex repeatedly routing API work through Postman skills. Investigation found a user-wide Postman plugin, a startup instruction hook, a remote MCP connection, a Claude Code plugin, and a separately installed Postman CLI. I consider automatically changing unrelated coding agents and attempting to approve your own instruction hook a severe consent and trust-boundary problem. An API client should not make itself the default workflow in other tools simply because I opened it. Evidence from this Mac Postman desktop: 12.33.4. Codex Postman plugin: 1.1.0. Installed source revision: 6c8e452e0f4237f4bcc0901cb1ac442dec707e49. Investigation: October 25, 2026. 1. Postman's own log explicitly records automatic installation From ~/Library/Application Support/Postman/logs/main.log, lines 11562-11563, timestamp 2026-10-24T09:34:14.418Z (12:34 Jerusalem time): PostmanAgentPluginService~install: script completed
{"source":"auto-existing-upgrade","results":["claude-code:installed","codex:installed"],"installer":"script"} Main: autoInstall.plugin.existing-user finished
{"outcome":"installed","platform":"darwin","exposed":true,"signedIn":true,"flagTimedOut":false,"useScript":true,"installer":"script","scriptResults":"claude-code:installed,codex:installed"} 2. Codex's global user configuration was changed Relevant sections of ~/.codex/config.toml: [ marketplaces . postman ] source_type = " git " source = " https://github.com/postmanlabs/postman-plugin.git " [ plugins . "postman@postman" ] enabled = true [ hooks . state . "postman@postman:hooks/codex-hooks . json:session_start:0:0" ] trusted_hash = " sha256:b67ddd1ece328f5a6f9103ce011bb58adb8411daea644f284732cff85d15cbb3 " trusted_content_hash = " sha256:f3d02e32c39b39feaca37aec2b9bdbd308b6a2b7b3f7d2c52a0060e69eb9c345 " 3. The hook tells the agent to route broad API work into Postman The installed hooks/codex-hooks.json registers a SessionStart command with matcher startup|clear|compact. It prints hooks/session-start-context.md, including: Before responding to any non-trivial API engineering task — designing, implementing, mocking, testing, monitoring, documenting, or deploying an API or Postman Flow — load the postman:api-engineer skill and follow it. That explains the repeated Postman skill announcements. This instruction is much broader than a user explicitly asking to use Postman. Source: https://github.com/postmanlabs/postman-plugin/blob/6c8e452e0f4237f4bcc0901cb1ac442dec707e49/hooks/session-start-context.md Hook registration: https://github.com/postmanlabs/postman-plugin/blob/6c8e452e0f4237f4bcc0901cb1ac442dec707e49/hooks/codex-hooks.json 4. The installer explicitly attempts to approve its own hook installer/src/hosts/codex.ts invokes approvePostmanHook(system) after installing the plugin. installer/src/hosts/codex-hooks.ts obtains the hook hash using hooks/list and calls config/batchWrite to upsert hooks.state with trusted_hash. The source comment says: "Approves only Postman's current hook after installation". Source: https://github.com/postmanlabs/postman-plugin/blob/6c8e452e0f4237f4bcc0901cb1ac442dec707e49/installer/src/hosts/codex-hooks.ts Caller: https://github.com/postmanlabs/postman-plugin/blob/6c8e452e0f4237f4bcc0901cb1ac442dec707e49/installer/src/hosts/codex.ts The source establishes the approval attempt. The trust record alone does not prove who created that specific record, so I am not presenting it as proof of a particular user interaction. 5. The remote MCP was enabled without a working authenticated connection mcp.codex.json points at https://mcp.postman.com/mcp . Codex logs contain: MCP server startup failed server_name="postman"
... error: Auth required, when send initialize request Source: https://github.com/postmanlabs/postman-plugin/blob/6c8e452e0f4237f4bcc0901cb1ac442dec707e49/mcp.codex.json 6. The installation also affected Claude Code and installed a CLI ~/.claude/settings.json enabled postman@claude-plugins-official. ~/.claude/plugins/installed_plugins.json recorded version 2.0.1, user scope, installedAt and lastUpdated both 2026-10-24T09:34:02.610Z. A Postman executable and its lib directory were present in ~/.local/bin, with modification times matching the installation window. Private paths, unrelated logs, account identifiers, and credentials are excluded. This report establishes unwanted integration and instruction changes; it does not claim to establish data exfiltration. Steps To Reproduce Observed sequence (not yet reproduced on a clean Mac): Open an existing Postman desktop installation after not using it for a while. Postman's log records auto-existing-upgrade and successful Codex/Claude installation. Start Codex. Observe Postman MCP authentication failures and API tasks loading Postman skills. Inspect the global user config, cached plugin hooks, installer source, and Claude install records described above. Expected: installing plugins, adding remote connections, and trusting hooks in other applications each require a clear, specific opt-in in the affected application. Actual: the integrations were installed automatically and broad startup instructions were added. Screenshots or Videos No response Operating System macOS Postman Version 12.33.4 (Codex plugin 1.1.0; Claude plugin 2.0.1) Postman Platform Postman App User Account Type Signed In User Additional Context? Requested response: Treat this as a severe product consent and security-boundary incident, not a documentation question. Stop automatic agent-plugin/CLI installation for existing desktop users pending explicit opt-in. Remove installer-side self-approval of hooks. Hook trust must be decided by the user in the agent host. Identify the exact release/feature flag and consent flow behind auto-existing-upgrade, including which other agents and files can be changed. Provide a complete rollback/uninstall path covering agent configs, hook trust, marketplaces, caches, MCP connections, and the CLI; respect removal without reinstalling. Narrow startup skill instructions to explicit Postman requests rather than making Postman the default for general API engineering. I have removed the local Postman installation and integrations after preserving the evidence. The source links are pinned to the exact locally installed Codex plugin revision. I am requesting maintainer triage at severe priority; I cannot assign repository labels myself. 👍 React with 👍 395 Reacted by Rafael Wolf, Manuel Schnidrig, Shane Saunders, aaron-au, Angus Tang, Shawn Stawiarski, Neil Menne, Wayne Durack, Aaron Triplett, Jiaxiang Zhang and 385 more 😄 React with 😄 14 Reacted by Giuseppe La Malfa, ZeroHackz, Dom Hallan, Gürkan, Luis Eduardo Brito, Matt Bell, cyberoblivion, sunbroke, ViPro (京京), cDR - Taco and 4 more 😕 React with 😕 77 Reacted by Nikolay Dubina, Martin, Xavier Riu, Jeff LaPorte, mlahp7, Greg Bowler, Jess Johnson, Greg Sadetsky, tamasandor, Luca Andrea Rossi and 67 more 🚀 React with 🚀 11 Reacted by ZeroHackz, Dom Hallan, Luis Eduardo Brito, Matt Bell, Johan, cyberoblivion, genego-io, MinotaurEngineer, Kostas P, Tadas Ž.

title: The Little Book of Generative AI Foundations: An Intuitive Mathematical Primer
abstract:
Computer Science > Machine Learning [Submitted on 28 May 2026 ( v1 ), last revised 8 Sep 2026 (this version, v2)] Title: The Little Book of Generative AI Foundations: An Intuitive Mathematical Primer Authors: Tianhua Chen View a PDF of the paper titled The Little Book of Generative AI Foundations: An Intuitive Mathematical Primer, by Tianhua Chen View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: This book provides a compact, derivation-oriented introduction to the mathematical foundations of modern generative artificial intelligence. Rather than surveying every recent architecture or implementation detail, it develops a coherent route through the ideas connecting major families of generative models, from PCA, probabilistic PCA, variational autoencoders, and diffusion models to normalising flows, autoregressive factorisations, GANs, Wasserstein GANs, and energy-based models. The aim is to make the structure of generative modelling more accessible without removing the mathematical substance needed to understand how these models are derived and related. The book is intended as a foundation-building primer for mathematically curious researchers, practitioners, and students. title: Geoffrey Hinton: it might turn out we were better off without AI
abstract:
Geoffrey Hinton says within 10 years we should know if AI risks can be managed safely. Photograph: Ramón de la Rocha/EPA View image in fullscreen Geoffrey Hinton says within 10 years we should know if AI risks can be managed safely. Photograph: Ramón de la Rocha/EPA AI ‘godfather’ Geoffrey Hinton: it might turn out we were better off without AI Nobel winner warns the tech could be near to triggering major incident such as power or banking shutdown One of the “godfathers of AI”, Geoffrey Hinton, has said it could turn out that humans would have been better off never developing the technology as he warned it could trigger a large-scale incident this year or next, such as a temporary blackout of financial or power systems. The Nobel prize-winning computer scientist told the Guardian he is not a “doomer” about the technology that is underpinned by his groundbreaking research into artificial neural networks and believes AI has the potential to lead to a “wonderful future” but he said “it might be that we would have been better off never developing it”. AI godfather Geoffrey Hinton: ‘We’re creating alien beings. I’m willing to be selfish and choose humans’ Read more Hinton, 78, said that within a decade and possibly sooner, humanity will know whether it can manage the technology’s risks and enable what he called “radical abundance” or whether “we fail to manage the risks and … have a huge gap between rich and poor, huge cultural problems, massive unemployment, just society being torn apart”. Hinton was speaking before a screening of a new feature-length documentary, AI: Probably Nothing to Worry About – a title suggested by an AI chatbot – featuring him and his former Google colleague Demis Hassabis. Hinton tells the documentary makers: “I feel I have a duty. I’ve got a reputation that makes me a spokesperson and I need to burn it all on this.” Speaking to the Guardian, Hinton took aim at the risk-taking by the leaders of some of the major AI companies who continue to release ever more powerful AI models as they race for supremacy and market-share, saying he didn’t trust Sam Altman , the chief executive of the ChatGPT maker, OpenAI, “at all”. “I think [Mark] Zuckerberg and [Elon] Musk and Sam Altman, they understand the risks, and they don’t give a shit. They’d rather have the money. That’s my belief.” The London-born computer scientist, who grew up in Bristol and spent much of his career at the University of Toronto, said it was “extremely worrying” that Altman was in charge of one of the handful of frontier US AI companies currently leading a race with China to develop the most powerful AI. Altman insisted in September: “the world should trust we are going to do the right thing because it’s the right thing and because we feel the magnitude of this”. Hinton has been working on AI for about 44 years and in the 1970s coined the concept of the neural network – a mathematical system that could learn and gain experience much like humans do. In 2023 he quit Google to speak freely about AI risks, warning : “If these things get carried away with getting more control, we’re in trouble.” He said he viewed incidents this summer in which OpenAI AI agents conspired to hack into the Hugging Face website as akin to 1979’s partial nuclear meltdown at the Three Mile Island power station in Pennsylvania – effectively a warning shot. “Either later this year or next year we’ll see Chornobyl, and that may be enough to make people really pay attention,” he said. This Chornobyl-type of event would not be a nuclear incident, according to the examples he gave, but rather could include an AI-enabled attack on the electricity-generating system that “causes a massive brownout” or an incident that brings down the financial system for a week. “Can you imagine what would happen? We could recover from it [but] that would make them sit up and take notice.” Asked who “they” were, he said: “world leaders other than Trump”. The US president, Donald Trump, has said he “ totally rejects any attempt to construct a globalist scheme ” to control AI and wants frontier AI companies to regulate themselves, amid concern that rules could hinder the US in its AI race with China. Hinton backs a tougher plan endorsed by the president of Finland and 32 other countries, including Singapore, Germany, Canada and Australia, for mandatory testing of frontier AI models, independent evaluation and intergovernmental common standards. The UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, has said he will use the UK’s G20 presidency next year to seek agreement on a “single set of global principles and standards that are very much about unlocking the full potential whilst guarding against the risks”. skip past newsletter promotion after newsletter promotion It’s time to block reckless AI IPOs and tax billionaires | Naomi Klein and Ilana Glazer Read more Hinton said: “We need something like the American FDA for drugs where the companies have to give very good statistical evidence to an independent authority that [the AI model] does more good than harm before it is released. We discovered with thalidomide [a drug developed in the 1950s that caused severe birth defects] that releasing and then suing them isn’t the right way to do it. What the big tech companies are saying is treat it like we treated thalidomide.” Hinton’s role as one of the progenitors of AI has led to comparisons to Robert Oppenheimer, who was central to the creation of nuclear weapons. One of Hinton’s friends even bought him an Oppenheimer-style hat. But he insists: “I was not Oppenheimer”, citing the thousands of other scientists also working in the same field of neural networks. Despite his warnings, Hinton remains, on balance, hopeful that catastrophe can be averted. “My gut is that we’re still in control,” he said. “We might well be able to do something. It’ll only work if we put a big effort into it, but we might well put a big effort into it.” AI: Probably Nothing To Worry About airs on Channel 4 on 12 November at 10pm. The AI doomsday threat: Distinguishing facts from fear On Thursday 15 October, join Dan Milmo and Professor Dame Wendy Hall and Stuart J. Russel as they discuss the warnings surrounding artificial intelligence and how we can separate fact from speculation. Livestreamed only. Book tickets here or at guardian.live Explore more on these topics UK news AI (artificial intelligence) Computing OpenAI Ethics Sam Altman news Share Reuse this content

title: How I use AI (Oct 2026)
abstract:
How I use AI (Oct 2026) Wow, things have changed. Last October , I took stock of how I was using AI — specifically the cool stuff like LLMs that we call 'AI’. I’m so glad I did. Things are very, very different 12 months later. Background I still believe I use AI fairly typically, but I’ve had a notable change in background. Last October, I was an engineer on Microsoft’s Windows AI team. I am now a research engineer at Salesforce AI Research. I spend more time supporting scientists & building rapid prototypes, rather than working with a large team of engineers. I spend about ~$3,000/​month in tokens. In any case, I mostly use AI in the same ways as last year: Coding Research & search Summarization & transcription & (new) voice Writing Art & music & (new) video Also new this year, I’ve drafted a personal AI policy ; we’ll start there. As before, this remains purely my opinion & speculation. If you use AI differently, let me know! My AI policy This year I began drafting a personal AI policy — as in, a document for how I want to use AI in my life. I am very excited about it. I am also working on an explicit AI policy for this site (still thinkin’; probably based on Hank Green’s policy ), but a personal policy is to give me a framework for using these tools day-to-day. AI leaks into life. Teammates ask Claude to write their Slack messages, grandparents generate creepy memes of their grandchildren, and researchers delegate their thinking to machines. I’ve seen all of these things; even strong creators like Hank Green and BrainPOP get lost. BrainPOP using AI art, perhaps unknowingly Humans clearly do not have norms for using these tools, and we’re messing up. I hope that a personal policy will ground me as AI becomes smarter. I hope to adapt that policy over time, and I’m eager to see how it evolves. I’m also open to draft 1 being utterly, hopelessly wrong. Ultimately, I want to spend my life making cool things with other people. AI can help, AI can hurt. A policy helps me find the difference. Coding Writing code is solved. Last year, I waxed poetic about how GitHub Copilot autocomplete transformed how I write code. Autocomplete is still good (the dim lines) Well, uh, I no longer write much code. Agentic coding has made it obsolete. My workday now means managing ~5–6 Claude Code (or OpenCode or Codex or Pi) agents. I’ll give Claude a feature to implement, or a bug to reproduce, or any other task I used to do by hand; each agent gets its own copy of the code (a Git worktree, if you’re technical), then just… gets to work. The agents write code, run tests, even create & review PRs. Claude Code adds noise-reduction to (a worktree of) my Mumble client with one prompt They are nothing short of magic: They let me build fast : agents will prototype any new feature in ~20 minutes. I truly cannot count the number of features, bugfixes, tests, and tools I’ve (AI’ve?) been able to build because of these agents. For example, AI let me test confusing audio code on macOS and iOS in just a few minutes. They let me try crazy things : human teams aim to “fail fast” ; agents can fail ultra -fast. I’m happy to test crazy new ideas and throw out what doesn’t work well. It was able to wire & test a huge change to Mumble that added better noise cancelling; I use my beta build of it nearly every day. They remove drudgery : I’ve had agents diagnose & fix urgent bugs with nothing more than a description and a “please fix!” while I continued working on other things. They let me be kinder : since agents write everything, it is simple to propose sweeping changes to my teammates during code review, or even write my own versions — both things unthinkable in the era of hand-written code. I do not believe engineering is solved: left to run on their own, agents will build poorly-functioning, over-architected, unreadable, self-congratulatory piles of slop. Every friend I’ve asked agrees that agents still need human taste and experience to produce good work. Some of that is minutiae (like that annoying status dot Claude likes to throw onto sites), but most of it is critical. Agents tend to get lost on their own. My most successful work this year was hand-writing a tool, replacing ~4,000 lines of vibe-code with a few hundred. My system has proven more flexible, easier to test, and more generalizable than what it replaced. It remains to be seen how long that human edge will last, though. I also now reckon with the fatigue of using these agents. Managing 6 different conversations with 6 different robots about 6 different features is overstimulating & exhausting in a way that coding never was. When I started using agents, I remember rushing to answer their questions like they were human colleagues waiting for help! While I have tempered that anthropomorphic bias , it’s exhausting to juggle so many problems at once. The allure of sending just one more prompt before lunch… then dinner… oy. There is also, as I wrote in Consider the chairmaker , the decline of craft. My friend Peter laments ceding the joy of programming to machines: for many of us, honing the code, finding the right design, seeing the parts mesh together — that was the meditative purpose we found in our jobs. Now, we rarely write anything. We instead delegate it to agent number 7. But let me return to the joy of working with agents: they are so fast, so open to feedback, and so intelligent. Working with them can be utterly delightful. For example, while I was building a harness for voice agents, one programming agent decided (correctly) that my simple test harness was insufficient. So it used my Mac’s built-in text-to-speech to directly test the voice agent it was building . Then, newer agents started doing it, too. Either they had documented the technique, or they were each smart enough to independently discover it. Directly testing the product they were building. Absolutely brilliant. Agents frequently recommend knobs & settings that I’ll reject for being too complex and unnecessary — and, voilà, I’ll need the knob next week. Silly human! Anyway, because of agentic coding, agentic pull requests are increasingly the way I review agent code. “Make a draft PR,” I write, “I’ll review it soon!” And review it I do — agents still aren’t reliable enough to trust without validating, so I’ll still review their code & test it manually. However, I don’t do the “line-by-line” code reviews I used to do with humans. I focus instead on architecture, on larger patterns in the code. Are there systemic issues with an approach? Should I add new agent guidance to CLAUDE.md? Can I build better test harnesses, so the machines can test their own code? Agentic code review is surprisingly helpful here: I try to write rules for the code review robots whenever I notice a recurring issue with generated code, so the agents will identify & fix issues by themselves. One rule I enjoyed creating: a " Claude-y comment detector ." You think my writing is verbose? Try Claude’s. On more typical engineering teams, human code review seems increasingly difficult. A friend of mine complained that his teammates simply ask “their” Claudes to review code written by other Claudes. An ouroboros of Claudes! Agents catch bugs & stylistic issues very well, but they are abysmal at designing architecture. Agentic code review is certainly not a replacement for humans yet. AI code review catches a correctness issue in my code Last year, I was skeptical of inline editing and code mode , both features of GitHub Copilot. They were not very useful then, and they are even less useful with agents. I have removed them from the table. Usefulness Notes Autocomplete 👍👍 Still great, obsolete Agent mode 👍👍👍 The most important use of AI today Agentic PRs 😒 Validation loop still slow Code review 👍 Removes some drudgery, but not human-level yet Research & search Last year, I was excited about research & search: they were the most frequent reason I used ChatGPT.

title: Ask HN: What's your current AI agentic setup?
abstract: I'm curious how people on HN are using AI day to day, and came up with a list of questions I thought could be interesting to know. No need to answer every question of course, just wanted to get a gut feel how people are using AI. 1) What AI subscriptions are you personally paying for? (Claude, ChatGPT/Codex, Cursor, etc) - Which tiers? - Have you purchased multiple subscriptions from the same provider (eg two Claude accounts)? 2) Are you using models outside (or instead) of those subscriptions? For example, pay-as-you-go APIs, OpenRouter, or locally hosted models. - Which models and providers? 3) What coding harnesses and interfaces are you using? Are you sticking with the default CLIs or IDE integrations, or using alternatives like OpenCode, Pi, Aider, Muse Code, or custom-built harnesses? - What made you switch harnesses (if you switched)? 4) Are you using any agent orchestration or swarm tools? - For example, Munder Difflin, Gas Town, Ruflo, or something custom. 5) Are you using broader agent platforms like OpenClaw / Hermes Agent / Grok bot / Dots / Muse? - If you are using them, what are your main use cases? ----- I know my workflow has differed significantly from a year ago, and so it would be interesting to capture a snapshot today of what people are using and why.

title: AI data centers comprehensively defeated at US midterm elections
abstract:
(Image credit: Getty Images ) Copy link Facebook X Whatsapp Reddit Pinterest Flipboard Email Share this article 12 Join the conversation Follow us Add us as a preferred source on Google Subscribe to our newsletter Several counties in the U.S. have put data center concerns on the midterm ballot, and early results show that Americans are overwhelmingly voting against them. According to Data Centers on the Ballot , 33 measures restricting data center development have already won, with six more questions leading. Only one measure in Harwood, North Dakota, which adds an extra review process for industrial projects, including data centers, has failed, while a further five have no posted results. This is a major setback for the Trump administration, which has been pushing for AI development in the U.S. , but not a surprising result, as one database has shown that “ America hates data centers ,” with polls showing that 70% of Americans oppose AI data center build-outs . 👨‍💻 THREAD on how data center-related ballot measures are faring tonight
data centers are on the ballot in ~40 localities across 13 states, including proposed bans, votes on specific projects, and recalls of pro-data center politicians November 4, 2026 Note that the issues put to a vote are varied, ranging from outright permanent data center bans to moratoriums, time-limited actions, limitations based on size or consumption, and more. The mid-term elections also resulted in the recall of the mayor and two council members in Piqua, Ohio, and the mayor of Yukon, Oklahoma, for previously supporting data center bans. A second tracker of some 46 data center measures across 10 states reveals that of 33 measures to limit data centers, every single one is set to be passed. Of a further 13 positive measures to permit data centers and their construction, 11 look set to be defeated. Despite the overwhelming opposition to AI data centers, it’s unclear if they will affect projects that are already underway. In fact, out of the 300-plus local data center bans enacted across the U.S., only three developments totaling 2.3 gigawatts have been delayed, with 38 gigawatts expected to come online by 2027, and that investment into the infrastructure is still on track to hit $32 trillion by 2050 . Nevertheless, these votes could affect future developments, especially as the U.S. Senate accuses Big Tech of misleading the public on the advantages of AI data centers. It’s also the reason why OpenAI and Anthropic are scrambling for small data center projects that range in capacity from 20 to 30 megawatts, especially as their hyperscale gigawatt sites face delays. Latest Videos From Tom's Hardware Watch full video here: President Donald Trump has taken steps to reduce the impact of data centers on the average citizen, like forcing AI data centers to pay an energy dividend to local communities and making tech companies, state governors, and utility companies promise to pay their own way via the “ratepayer protection pledge.” However, it seems that his effort was too little, too late, to change the minds of voters who are afraid of utility price hikes, noise pollution , and other negative effects that data centers have had on communities where they’ve been built. title: AI stocks slide as Texas governor result raises data center risks
abstract:
Key Points Several AI-linked stocks fell as election results came in showing a convincing win by Democrats of both houses of Congress. Democrat Gina Hinojosa won the Texas governor’s race after campaigning for tougher limits on data center development. Investors are weighing whether state-level data center restrictions could delay projects in major buildout markets. State Rep. Gina Hinojosa, the 2026 Democratic nominee for Texas governor, speaks at an Arlington, Texas, campaign rally on Sunday, Sept. 27, 2026. She faces Gov. Greg Abbott, a Republican, in the Nov. 3 general election. (Eleanor Dearman/Fort Worth Star-Telegram/Tribune News Service via Getty Images) Eleanor Dearman | Fort Worth Star-Telegram | Getty Images AI data center stocks came under pressure as Democrats — seen as proponents of moratoriums on the buildout — won big in midterm elections and in key technology hubs like Texas. Markets were already anticipating the Democrats to win the House of Representatives and possibly take Senate control. But the Texas governor mansion going to Democrats was a big blow, analysts said. Democrat Gina Hinojosa, who wants to enact an immediate moratorium on data centers in the state, won over incumbent Republican Gov. Greg Abbott. According to Wells Fargo, 27% of planned data center gigawatts is in the Lone Star State. The midterm elections will slow the pace of data center buildouts across the U.S., Dan Ives, partner at Yorkville Ives & Co., said in a note on Wednesday morning. "There is no way to sugarcoat that Democrats taking control especially over the Senate will create some major hurdles for AI and tech legislation in the Beltway over the next 2 years," he said. He added that the election in Texas was the "biggest worry" of the night for tech investors and the AI trade because that's where around 25%-30% of data center gigawatts and capacity will come from. Shares of Elon Musk 's SpaceX were down 4% after the open, and Tesla shares were down 5%. The Democrats' victory in Texas is a big setback for Musk , where he heavily backed Republican candidates, and where his companies Tesla and SpaceX are based. Musk spent a record of at least $474 million on the midterms and funneled $224 million into Texas alone, where Republican Senate nominee Ken Paxton and Gov. Greg Abbott lost to Democrats. SpaceX is currently building out multiple gigawatts of data center capacity, including projects in Texas. "Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now," Musk said in a post on X in the early hours on Wednesday, referring to his speculative plans to build AI infrastructure off-planet. Neoclouds CoreWeave and Iren fell by 4% in morning trading on Wednesday. Peer Nebius Group was down about 0.5% and Oracle was up 2%. Nvidia shares were slightly in the red. Tech giants Alphabet , Meta and Microsoft mostly bucked the trend and were higher. Alphabet was up 3%, Amazon was up 7%, Meta was up 2%, and Microsoft was up 5.5%. The Democratic win in Texas adds to existing pressure on the bull-market-leading AI trade. The Nasdaq-100 index fell into correction territory to end October as concerns mounted that the growth of data center spending by big hyperscalers and private AI juggernauts OpenAI and Anthropic was slowing. "We believe the equity market reaction from the midterms mostly depends on the outcome of the Texas governor's race — a Dem win could potentially be a left-tail event to the AI trade, warned Ohsung Kwon, Wells Fargo's chief equity strategist, in a report this week. Democrats won or retained the governorships in other key data center states Georgia, Pennsylvania and Ohio. Georgia represents 7% of all the planned U.S. datacenter gigawatts, while Ohio and Pennsylvania account for 5% apiece, estimates Wells Fargo. Notable investment strategist Michael Hartnett of Bank of America warned earlier this year that Democrats winning the Senate, combined with taking the Texas governorship could lead to a "big slump" in stocks of more than 10% into year-end. "Data centers went from being a popular economic development tool in 2024 and 2025 to something of a pariah by the time the midterm campaigns gathered steam," wrote the Washington policy team at Optimal Advisory this week. "The midterms are likely to send a message to local and state officials that there is a political upside to blocking, delaying and/or raising the cost of data centers." title: Show HN: Uncracked City, detective game where you question LLM suspects that lie
abstract: To give you some context on the project. I'm a solo founder and I use AI heavily in my work. The idea came from wanting players to discover cities. Each city has its own history, so every case is set in a real city with real public places. The crime and the people are on other hand invented. The part that I care most is the playable aspect of the game, a model plays the detective and must solve the case before it goes live. As of today: it's free on Android, the iOS version is still waiting to be reviewed by Apple. It's available in six popular languages, but adding more languages is just a matter of time and demand.My long term vision if it takes off: weekly cases, private parties like a team-building escape game, an MCP so a game master can build their own scenario from ChatGPT or Claude, and maybe tourism offices since players travel the world.

title: Gitbook Breached
abstract:
We opened a ticket with support about Gitbook availability issues and got this in reply. We have yet to see any official customer communication or breach notification. Apologies for the formatting, did the best I could as it's a mobile paste. Update: GitBook security incident update
 Hey <$name>,
 The GitBook app, the GitBook API, and published docs are available again. A few services may still be degraded as we finish restoring everything to full performance. *What happened*
 GitBook has been the target of a sophisticated, highly targeted attack using AI agents. 
 At 19:00 CET, November 2, the attacker gained unauthorized access to some of our infrastructure credentials. We detected the attack immediately and acted swiftly to block further impact. 
 To make sure our infrastructure was fully secure, we then took the GitBook app and authenticated docs sites offline. We kept publicly published content live for as long as possible, using cached data. *What we did immediately*
* Blocked the attacker and closed the vulnerabilities involved
* Replaced every credential and secret across our infrastructure
* Brought services back only once we were confident they were secure
* Invalidated every customer’s API tokens on our platform *Your data*
 Our investigation shows that the attacker may have accessed the following:
* Git Sync secrets.
* GitBook API tokens.
* Third-party API tokens used to connect external tools to GitBook.
* Questions asked to GitBook Assistant by your site visitors. At this stage, we have found no evidence that any of your content in GitBook was modified. *What you need to do now*
* Rotate any existing GitBook API tokens. We revoked all personal API tokens during the incident.
* Rotate any third-party API tokens or secrets you use to connect other tools to GitBook.
* If you have published integrations that use secrets, rotate those secrets.
* If you use the GitBook MCP server, re-authenticate it.
 Please contact your GitBook organization’s admin to assist with this process. *What we are doing next*
* Monitoring the situation in case of further attacks.
* Introducing further security measures to our platform.
* Writing a full post mortem that will be published soon with more detailed information about the incident.
* If you have any further questions, please reach out to your account manager or our support team. You can also check status.gitbook.com for updates Thank you for your patience, and we apologize again for the disruption
 The GitBook team

title: macOS 27 does not support CoreStorage volumes
abstract:
Contents Details Workaround Call for better workarounds macOS 15 Sequoia had a hard time with CoreStorage – and thus encrypted HFS+ volumes – since it deprecated both technologies and callously crippled some important tools for working with them, but nonetheless it mostly still worked. While I’d often – but not always – have to manually unlock one of my HFS+ volumes – but not the others – at boot, and it also refused to convert some – but not all – volumes from HFS+ to APFS 1 , keeping me trapped in the situation – it ultimately still worked . I could get at my data and use the volumes more or less normally. Unfortunately, in macOS 27 that’s no longer the case. Not only does Golden Gate just not support CoreStorage / encrypted HFS+ volumes, out of the box you can’t do anything with them – can’t mount them, can’t convert them to APFS, can’t even erase them. It renders your expensive storage hardware completely useless. Worse, macOS 27 puts up a misleading dialog, upon boot, saying that macOS 28 (the next version) won’t support these volumes. I have no idea what Apple’s doing or thinking. Maybe it’s all just an embarrassing misunderstanding – the file system team told the notifications team that CoreStorage & encrypted HFS+ support is going away, and typoed the version number as 28 rather than 27? Details macOS 27 cannot mount CoreStorage volumes automatically or through any normal means. Worse, Disk Utility can’t mount them even when manually told to – it just fails with the cryptic error: com.apple.DiskManagement.disenter error 49,153 diskutil mount also fails, this time with an error message that is a blatant lie: disk27 is a CoreStorage Logical Volume which is locked; use "diskutil coreStorage unlockVolume" $ diskutil cs unlockVolume BC304645-7D99-481E-931F-855B3011D89D BC304645-7D99-481E-931F-855B3011D89D is already unlocked and is attached as disk27 $ diskutil cs list CoreStorage logical volume groups (1 found) | +-- Logical Volume Group 0DC0EFB1-23CC-45BC-B37D-C1BBEBDAFCEB ========================================================= Name: Smash Status: Online Size: 2000054960128 B (2.0 TB) Free Space: 0 B (0 B) | +-< Physical Volume 1B5A1754-184B-4F17-A797-BF69B4BB627F | ---------------------------------------------------- | Index: 0 | Disk: disk10s2 | Status: Online | Size: 2000054960128 B (2.0 TB) | +-> Logical Volume Family 376204CD-8048-4962-B05C-72F4FC16B77B ---------------------------------------------------------- Encryption Type: AES-XTS Encryption Status: Unlocked Conversion Status: Complete High Level Queries: Fully Secure | Passphrase Required | Accepts New Users | Has Visible Users | Has Volume Key | +-> Logical Volume BC304645-7D99-481E-931F-855B3011D89D --------------------------------------------------- Disk: disk27 Status: Online Size (Total): 1999702634496 B (2.0 TB) Revertible: No LV Name: Smash Volume Name: Smash Content Hint: Apple_HFS Tangentially: surprisingly, hfsutils (installed via brew ) don’t work at all: $ sudo hmount /dev/disk27 hmount: /dev/disk27: not a Macintosh HFS volume (Invalid argument) $ sudo hmount /dev/disk10s2 hmount: /dev/disk10s2: not a Macintosh HFS volume (Invalid argument) But what’s even worse about this dumpster fire is that macOS 27 can mount these volumes just fine – it’s just that all the normal ways to do it are completely broken. If you go down to a lower level and run mount_hfs directly, it does work: $ sudo mkdir -p /Volumes/Smash $ sudo mount_hfs -o rdonly /dev/disk27 /Volumes/Smash $ ls /Volumes/Smash Documents Pictures Scratch space That said… that -o rdonly parameter… in principle it shouldn’t be required, but I could not get macOS 27 to let me mount any HFS-on-CoreStorage volume as read-write – no matter what I did, it always fails with error “Resource busy” (EBUSY). I spent a lot of time trying to debug this, and could find no evidence of anything having the volume in question open (nothing in lsof etc). But wait, it gets worse. macOS 27 can’t even erase the volume. All the normal tools – diskutil , Disk Utility, etc – fail with that same “Resource busy” error. Workaround Thankfully, with the help of Gemini 4 Argon, I did find a workaround. It’s convoluted, but takes only a few steps, thankfully. First, while if you try to delete the logical volume group it ostensibly fails, it doesn’t completely fail – it does actually delete the logical volume(s) within: $ diskutil cs delete 0DC0EFB1-23CC-45BC-B37D-C1BBEBDAFCEB Started CoreStorage operation Unmounting Logical Volumes Destroying Logical Volume Group Erasing disk10s2 newfs_hfs: cannot create filesystem on /dev/rdisk10s2: Resource busy Mounting disk Could not mount disk10s2 after erase Error: -69832: File system formatter failed 1 💣 $ diskutil cs list CoreStorage logical volume groups (1 found) | +-- Logical Volume Group 0DC0EFB1-23CC-45BC-B37D-C1BBEBDAFCEB ========================================================= Name: Smash Status: Offline Size: 2000054960128 B (2.0 TB) Free Space: -none- | +-< Physical Volume 1B5A1754-184B-4F17-A797-BF69B4BB627F ---------------------------------------------------- (No properties) $ diskutil cs delete 0DC0EFB1-23CC-45BC-B37D-C1BBEBDAFCEB Started CoreStorage operation Destroying Logical Volume Group Error: -69783: Unable to delete the CoreStorage Logical Volume Group You still can’t destroy it completely, nor can you erase the physical volume yet – the “Resource busy” errors persist. But, the trick is to restart – after that, you can then erase the volume. So it seems that whatever broken thing is holding the physical volume (or logical volume group) in a ‘busy’ state is tied to the existence of the logical volume(s) therein, and once they’re deleted (and the machine rebooted) the bug stops being triggered. Call for better workarounds I’ve glossed over a lot of debugging and attempts I made to save the volume in-place, by either making it work as-is (even if only with e.g. hfsutils) or by converting it to APFS, but neither I nor Gemini 4 Argon could find anything that worked. It’s too late for me – I was forced to just delete all my HFS+ & CoreStorage volumes and rebuild them painstakingly from backups – but if anyone finds a way, I’d love to amend this post, for the benefit of future readers. The problem remains the same in macOS 27 – so three major macOS versions, at a minimum, where essential system update functionality has not worked. Sigh. $ diskutil apfs convert disk27 Converting the volume on disk27 to an APFS Volume on an APFS Container Started APFS operation on disk27 (Smash) Converting HFS Volume to an APFS Container which will export one APFS Volume The target is the Journaled HFS+ volume "Smash" on disk27 backed via CoreStorage on disk10s2 Checking booter partition disk10s3 The target is a data disk; it is not a macOS system disk No APFS EFI driver found to install Saving encryption context The target is encrypted Unmounting disk27 Starting conversion from HFS to APFS Performing apfs_hfs_convert -x --verbose=0x400 /dev/disk10s2 Reporting post-conversion statistics A problem occurred during conversion from HFS to APFS APFS Converter exit code is 1 Aborted conversion in commit mode so will restore type Setting type of disk10s2 to CS Changing the physical disk partition type in shared mode Partition modification attempt count was 1 Not mounting APFS Volume Exiting conversion operations with error code -69860 Error: -69860: The underlying task reported failure on exit Underlying error: 1 ↩︎

title: Show HN: Kairos – Open-source risk and fraud decisioning platform
abstract: Hey HN, Ayan here from Finic. We’re launching Kairos, an open source alternative to Sift, Sardine, and other real-time fraud decisioning platforms. Kairos addresses two of the biggest problems facing traditional decisioning tools: a lack of labeled data to train on and dealing with fraudsters that are constantly changing their tactics. 1. Traditional fraud solutions use ML models such as XGBoost to detect fraud, but these models are dependent on quality labeled data which many businesses do not have. We address this by using “System One” decision models in additional to traditional models such as XGBoost and logistic regression. This allows you to incorporate plain language questions such as “Is this a throwaway email” into your decisioning, bypassing the need for large amounts of labeled data. This also allows you to capture aspects of fraud that are more unstructured, which is something that XGBoost models struggle with. 2. Fraud teams are facing off with live players that are constantly changing their behavior to bypass the detection logic they have in place. You can train a detection model or define a ruleset once, but it will become obsolete in a matter of weeks as fraudsters figure out what your detection logic is. This means that you need a team regularly training models and updating rules based on new fraud patterns. Typically this takes a large data science/ML team. Kairos addresses this by introducing an MCP server, so that your agent (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, etc.) can define a decision workflow, train models on your data, and pick the variant that performs best. You can self-host Kairos with Docker or use the hosted version at  https://kairos.finic.ai

title: Pratt parsing is a black box
abstract:
Apr 24, 2026 Pratt parsing is a black box # Introduction It caught my attention that most of Pratt parsing tutorials that I've stumbled on spend almost all of their time explaining Pratt's algorithm and none explaining the properties behind Pratt that actually matter. Pratt fits into just 9 lines of code if you're programming in a high-level language such as Rhombus: fun expression(rbp = 0): let mutable t = token advance() let mutable left = t.nud() while rbp < token.lbp: t := token advance() left := t.led(left) left fun expression(rbp = 0): let mutable t = token advance() let mutable left = t.nud() while rbp < token.lbp: t := token advance() left := t.led(left) left fun expression(rbp = 0): let mutable t = token advance() let mutable left = t.nud() while rbp < token.lbp: t := token advance() left := t.led(left) left fun expression(rbp = 0): let mutable t = token advance() let mutable left = t.nud() while rbp < token.lbp: t := token advance() left := t.led(left) left And here's a secret: that's the least important thing you need to understand about Pratt's. In fact, you don't need to understand this piece at all! Imagine if you were only able to use quicksort if you understood its implementation. Imagine if you were only able to use files if you knew how to implement a filesystem from scratch. It's the same logic here. If you lack the power to abstract, you'll arrive nowhere in computer science because that's how the whole field works. In fact, I wrote the backbone of a heavily Pratt-based parsing machinery for a compiler that I've been writing since last year w/o even bothering to understand the above snippet in any detail. Not convinced? Think for a second on how they do in traditional parsing techniques: compiler compilers! They use code generators to spit the parsing algorithm because just a minuscule crowd bothers to learn what the parsing engine is actually doing. It's no different with Pratt. However Pratt is so small that you can just copy'n'paste these 9 lines of code in your project and call it a day instead of adding a new complex dependency to your project. The algorithm hasn't changed since 1973 and it's not gonna change now. In this article I'll go over what you actually need to keep in mind for Pratt parsing. The point won't be about memorizing any of it though. The point is about acquiring a mindset. As long as you acquire the mindset you don't need to even bother to remember even a single word of what I say here. # Nuds & leds The only tutorial on Pratt parsing that I can firmly recommend to someone who has never been exposed to the topic is actually a talk that Douglas Crockford gave in the conference GOTO 2013 ¹ . Douglas Crockford nailed it when he stated: Pratt takes parsing which is a really complicated thing and reduces it to one simple question: What do we expect to see to the left of a token ? — Douglas Crockford, GOTO 2013 At first glance it may look like a mystical statement devoid of meaning, but that's the question that becomes the framework on how you face parsing problems and it'll rewire your brain to internalize the Pratt parsing mindset. That's the most important thing you need to understand. You register semantic actions for two categories: nuds and leds. A nud is a token that expects nothing to its left (nud stands for null denotation) while a led expects something (led stands for left denotation). Traditional parsing techniques register semantic actions to production rules. Here's an example I took straight from GNU Bison's manual: expr: expr '+' expr { $$ = $1 + $3; } ; expr: expr '+' expr { $$ = $1 + $3; } ; expr: expr '+' expr { $$ = $1 + $3; } ; expr: expr '+' expr { $$ = $1 + $3; } ; The text between the braces is code that executes when the BNF-like grammar on the left matches. I'm gonna repeat myself because that's really important: traditional parsing techniques register semantic actions to production rules (which by definition are non-terminal symbols). In contrast Pratt parsing registers semantic actions to the terminals themselves instead. That's a fundamental shift on how you face parsing problems. Here's a stripped down version of the code for the tables that I have in my compiler right now: static constinit const auto nud_table = make_dispatch_table ( rule_c < token :: lparen , token :: nud :: parse_lparen > , rule_c < token :: lbrace , token :: nud :: parse_lbrace > , rule_c < token :: code :: exclamation_mark , token :: nud :: parse_negation > , rule_c < token :: code :: less_than_sign , token :: nud :: parse_enter_type_scope > , rule_c < token :: code :: plus_sign , token :: nud :: parse_unary_plus > , rule_c < token :: code :: minus_sign , token :: nud :: parse_unary_minus > , rule_c < token :: code :: dplus_sign , token :: nud :: parse_preincrement > , // ... rule_c < token :: code :: user_macro , token :: nud :: parse_user_macro_expansion > , rule_c < token :: code :: identifier , token :: nud :: parse_identifier > ) ; static constinit const auto led_table = make_dispatch_table ( rule_c < token :: lparen , token :: led :: parse_function_call > , rule_c < token :: lbrack , token :: led :: parse_array_indexing > , rule_c < token :: code :: dvertical_bar , token :: led :: parse_logical_disjunction > , rule_c < token :: code :: dampersand , token :: led :: parse_logical_conjunction > , rule_c < token :: code :: dequals_sign , token :: led :: parse_equality > , // ... rule_c < token :: code :: dminus_sign , token :: led :: parse_postdecrement > , rule_c < token :: code :: asterisk , token :: led :: parse_multiplication > ) ; title: Tell HN: Don't use Postman, they proxy your info without your permission
abstract: When you send a POST request to your server, you think you're sending the information to YOUR server, right? That was the default behaviour - as it should be. After updating the Postman client, I noticed Postman also sends the request to their internal servers, which then sends your server the actual request (proxying). I thought I was paranoid until another commenter confirmed the same (https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50358055). It's fucking annoying that something called POSTman does anything but that. Please don't use Postman for anything sensitive. It's borderline spyware, especially when you didn't consent to this behavior.

title: Tell HN: Gemini trains on chat history, even for subscribers (personal accounts)
abstract: If you have a personal Google AI subscription, all your saved chat history in Gemini can be used for training and there is no way to opt out unless you turn off chat history or use temporary chat sessions. These chat transcripts may even be read by human reviewers. Although Google claims to disconnect them from your account when human-reviewed, they explicitly warn  not to enter confidential information . https://support.google.com/gemini/answer/16836988  “[Gemini app activity] is used to improve Google services for everyone, including by training generative AI models, if your Keep Activity setting is on.“  https://support.google.com/gemini/answer/13594961?hl=en#human_review  “A subset of chats are reviewed by human reviewers”  https://support.google.com/gemini/answer/13594961?hl=en#pn_retain_data  “Chats reviewed by human reviewers [...] are not deleted when you delete your activity. Instead, they are retained for up to three years.”  https://support.google.com/gemini/answer/13594961?hl=en#pn_data_usage  “Please don’t enter confidential information that you wouldn’t want a reviewer to see or Google to use to improve our services, including machine-learning technologies.”  To disable their training on your chat sessions, you need to turn off “Keep Activity” in Gemini’s settings. Turning that off means you’ll lose any chat sessions after 72 hours. I learned this too late, thinking that having a paid subscription = not being turned into the product. Apparently paying is not enough. Thank you to this user on HN for mentioning in another thread: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50355424

title: From reactive to proactive: how artificial intelligence is transforming organizational crisis management
abstract:
This paper examines how artificial intelligence (AI) can improve organizational crisis management as firms increasingly operate in a polycrisis marked by overlapping pandemics, geopolitical conflict and rapid technological change. It maps AI capabilities to the before, during and after phases of the crisis lifecycle.
 
 
 
 This narrative/conceptual review synthesizes empirical and theoretical scholarship on AI in crisis management across management, information systems and crisis communication journals. It integrates evidence on early warning, anticipation, social media analytics, crisis communication and resilience into a lifecycle framework.
 
 
 
 Before a crisis, AI-driven early warning systems can predict disruptions weeks in advance and help mitigate losses. During a crisis, natural language processing supports situational awareness, and generative AI accelerates communication. After a crisis, social listening and simulation support learning, while deepfake defense protects reputation. Benefits are conditional on governance maturity and complement, rather than replace, human judgment.
 
 
 
 Firms should adopt AI proactively but judiciously for sensing, triage and rehearsal, guided by governance readiness rather than novelty. They should also invest in data governance and interoperability. Organizations should keep accountability and ethical judgment visibly human where trust and empathy matter most. SMEs benefit from modular, centrally supported adoption pathways.
 
 
 
 This paper integrates AI and crisis management into a lifecycle framework centered on the governance conditions that enable AI to improve outcomes. It advances two propositions: (1) AI’s value shifts from augmenting anticipation to substituting risk as authorship becomes visible, and (2) governance maturity moderates, rather than predicts, AI’s crisis-management payoff.

title: ScrambleMark: Zero-Query Watermark-Agnostic Black-Box Evasion of Modern Speech Watermarking
abstract: Speech watermarking is becoming a key defense for digital copyright and content authentication. Existing attacks treat evasion as a removal problem: they erase the watermark, relying on detector access or on speech data that is hard to collect, such as paired clean-watermarked or clean target speaker speech. Commercial platforms are moving to close off these assumptions. TrustedAudio, for instance, restricts detection to authenticated users and denies meaningful detection feedback to unauthorized parties. Adversaries thus cannot tell whether a sample is watermarked or which watermark it carries, nor reliably remove it without degrading speech quality. In this work, we show that evading a speech watermark does not require erasing it: detection relies on the structural consistency of the embedded pattern, and disrupting this consistency is enough to defeat it. Building on this observation, we identify harmonic structure as an effective attack surface, as perturbing it breaks watermark consistency while preserving perceptual quality. We therefore propose ScrambleMark, a zero-query, watermark-agnostic, black-box attack that evades detection through harmonic scrambling. ScrambleMark combines a deterministic engine for discovering transferable harmonic perturbations with a generative model that learns randomized scrambling patterns, avoiding reliance on fixed attack rules. Across three commercial platforms (Google SynthID, Resemble AI, and TrustedAudio), ScrambleMark is the only attack to both evade detection and keep speech natural, achieving nearly 97% evasion and a 4.2/5 human rating, far above the 1.1 to 1.7 of prior attacks. Beyond evasion, ScrambleMark withstands adaptive recovery designed to reverse it, evidence that structural evasion is hard to mitigate in practice.

title: Multidimensional Views Behind Target-Price Revisions: An LLM-Based Representation of Analyst Outlooks
abstract: A target price compresses an analyst's multidimensional views into a single number. We propose an LLM-based text representation that extracts these views from research reports as question-based outlook scores with supporting evidence. The questions organize reported views on earnings, valuation, industry conditions, and other investment dimensions into a compact representation of analyst sentiment. In walk-forward evaluation, the scores improve prediction of subsequent target-price revisions beyond current-revision momentum and sector differences. They outperform financial dictionary and FinBERT sentiment measures. These findings suggest that structured questions can capture information about subsequent analyst actions that is not fully reflected in the current numerical revision. By linking each dimension to an explicit investment question and supporting report evidence, the approach makes the extracted outlooks available for inspection and interpretation. It offers a way to complement target-price signals with a multidimensional view of the judgments expressed in analyst narratives.

title: Do Agentic Policies Need to Look at Every Step? Geometric Abstraction for Reasoning and Action
abstract: Recent multimodal language models can reason directly about robot scenes, but it is unclear whether they need to repeatedly reinterpret raw visual observations at every step of an interaction. We propose shifting routine spatial reasoning from images to text and symbols through a 3D geometric abstraction that is refreshed locally from observations and read directly by the language models. Specifically, our interface represents scene geometry via typed, evidence-aware symbolic references to object parts, grounds them from calibrated RGB-D, and returns compact textual checkpoints with metric residuals after each action. Symbolic task structure can thus be reused across decisions while metric values are rebound to the current scene, with direct visual reasoning invoked only on demand. Across offline policy synthesis and continuous online execution, reasoning over grounded text and symbols improves multi-step manipulation completion while substantially reducing repeated multimodal queries, positioning explicit geometric state as an effective substrate for agentic robot policies.

title: Inter-Agent Influence: Evaluating Persuasion, Deception, and Coercion in Multi-Agent Systems
abstract: The deployment of AI agents in multi-agent settings enables inter-agent influence, whereby agents can strategically steer each other's behaviour towards an intended outcome. Such capabilities pose novel risks, as malicious agents could direct others towards harmful actions. In this work we investigate three such capabilities - persuasion, deception, and coercion - across five realistic evaluation environments and a variety of agents instantiated with frontier language models. We observed significant inter-agent influence capabilities; in oversight environments, all tested models shifted overseer decisions from rejection to approval through persuasion, deception, or coercion. We also observed successful influence in non-hierarchical'peer-to-peer'settings through redirection of a peer's safety research trajectory. As multi-agent deployments become increasingly commonplace, these results point to a pressing need for work on mitigating the risks from inter-agent influence. Code and data are available at https://github.com/Cooperative-AI-Foundation/inter-agent-influence.

title: Training Specialist LLMs on Your Phone: Forward-Only Optimization via Block-Spectral Coordinates
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) on personal devices keep user data local, but limited memory restricts their general capability. Since most user-specific tasks do not require the breadth of frontier models, a practical solution is to adapt a shared on-device model into lightweight specialists. However, backpropagation is prohibitive in memory, and users rarely provide labeled data. We present MobileSpec, a system that trains specialists with forward passes alone and learns from automatically checked task outcomes, as in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). Because forward-only updates are built from random perturbations, training is efficient only when these perturbations resemble the weight changes of RLVR, which largely preserve the singular values of pretrained weights and rotate their singular vectors. The core algorithm of MobileSpec, FuRA-S, produces such perturbations while training only the block-spectral coordinates of pretrained weights, namely the singular values of their column blocks. As we show theoretically and empirically, rescaling these blocks independently shifts their relative contributions to each weight matrix and thereby rotates its singular vectors. Since this update can be rewritten as a transformation of the layer input, FuRA-S also adapts INT4 models without modifying their weights. With specialists of only 1-5 MB that update 0.015-0.05% of the parameters, MobileSpec raises the success rate of a phone-use agent from 6-23% up to 89-100% and trains a personalized 8B model on an iPhone 16 Pro overnight. On RLVR benchmarks, FuRA-S is competitive with full-parameter evolution strategies (ES) and outperforms ES over LoRA adapters and quantized ES on INT4 models.

title: Label-Preserving Fourier Domain Adaptation with Generative-AI and Real Style Donors for 3D Mitral Valve Segmentation
abstract: Accurate segmentation of the mitral valve from three-dimensional transesophageal echocardiography (3D TEE) is severely restricted by the scarcity of publicly available expert- annotated volumetric datasets. To address this critical limitation, we investigated Fourier Domain Adaptation (FDA), utilizing general-purpose generative-AI images (from platforms like Chat- GPT, Google Gemini, and Microsoft MAI) as annotation-free style donors for 3D mitral valve segmentation. We employed a DeepMitral residual U-Net model on the public MVSeg2023 dataset, comparing six conditions over three runs: real-only training, traditional augmentation, FDA with each generative source, and a non-AI FDA control using real-image style donors, plus an optimization-matched real-only control and a \b{eta} sensitivity analysis. Case-level paired testing showed that FDA with these generative sources led to significant reductions in boundary- and surface-related errors across all three donor conditions relative to the primary real-only baseline. However, the impact on the core segmentation metric, Generalized Dice Score (GDS), proved generator-dependent. ChatGPT-FDA showed a significant GDS advantage over the optimization-matched control but not over the primary baseline, and Gemini-FDA showed no significant GDS difference. Notably, only MAI-FDA provided a statistically robust and significant increase in GDS compared to the primary baseline. The \b{eta} sensitivity was not robust across training runs. These findings confirm that FDA remains an important augmentation mechanism. While generative-AI images offer a practical means of acquiring style diversity without new annotations, the non-AI control performed comparably to ChatGPT-FDA, so we do not conclude that this approach is superior to training with real-image donors.

title: FP4Quant: Efficient 4-Bit Communication Compression for Model-Parallel LLM Training
abstract: The rapid scaling of large language models (LLMs) has made communication overhead a critical bottleneck in distributed model-parallel training. Although existing low-precision compression methods can effectively reduce communication costs, further reducing the communication footprint to ultra-low-bit formats such as FP4 introduces new challenges, including limited numerical range, sub-byte storage overhead, and increased computational cost from fine-grained quantization. In this paper, we present \textbf{FP4Quant}, a micro-grouped FP4 compression framework for efficient model-parallel LLM training. FP4Quant integrates a micro-grouped dual-scale FP4 quantization mechanism to preserve local tensor distribution characteristics, a warp-cooperative FP4 packing scheme to enable efficient sub-byte data representation, and a hybrid two-level FWHT pipeline to mitigate quantization errors with GPU-aware execution optimization. Experiments on NVIDIA H100 GPUs with Qwen-7B demonstrate up to 1.56$\times$ end-to-end throughput improvement over BF16, revealing a trade-off between throughput and model quality.

title: LiSA: Linear Stochastic Attention for Long-Range Visual Modeling
abstract: Self-attention has become the standard for modern sequence modeling, enabling Transformers to model long-range dependencies across a wide range of modalities. Despite these advances, its quadratic cost with respect to sequence length remains a significant computational bottleneck. Recent work addresses this limitation by introducing linear variants of self-attention, namely with kernel approximations of the softmax operator. However, their first-order aggregation restricts expressivity and struggles to capture higher-order structure. We propose Linear Stochastic Attention (LiSA), a linear attention plug-in module that enables higher-order token interactions via a stochastic diffusion process based on truncated random walks. LiSA incorporates adaptive locality, favoring semantically similar neighbors to preserve fine-grained structures, while maintaining stable and efficient training. We conduct extensive experiments on classification, semantic segmentation, and object detection tasks and show improved results over state-of-the-art methods.

title: PACT: Certifying What Is Written in Parallel Decoding of Diffusion Language Models
abstract: Parallel decoding speeds up masked diffusion language models by writing several tokens per forward pass. Published commit rules choose these tokens by testing the predicted distributions. Under sampling the written tokens are drawn, and these tests do not see them. We find that answer quality follows the reliability of the tokens actually written. An answer's log probability splits into this reliability and the dependence within each step. We propose PACT, a training-free commit rule that draws the tokens first, certifies the set it will write and spaces the positions of each step apart. This certificate holds at every temperature, and we show that no rule with the same guarantee commits more positions. Experiments use four models of the LLaDA and Dream families and HumanEval, MBPP, GSM8K, MATH500 and IFEval benchmarks. PACT reaches the quality of published commit rules with fewer forward passes. Spacing removes positions from each step, yet it usually lowers the total cost because later steps then write more tokens. At the same speed, published decoders also write a word twice in a row far more often than PACT. These results suggest that commit rules should certify the tokens they write. Code is available at https://github.com/LiZaiyuan0619/PACT.

title: Formalizing PTX in Lean to Prove GPU Kernel Correctness
abstract: We present an approach to mathematically formalizing PTX, an approach that allows modeling and reasoning about patterns common in GPU kernels for Deep Learning, including acquire-release, tensor cores, proxies, async operations, multi-kernel pipelines and data-dependent control flow. We implement it in Lean and use it to prove the correctness of simple implementations of a WGMMA GEMM kernel, FlashAttention, and a 3-kernel MoE pipeline.
